utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment. Yes. We have the witness here, so let's begin by having the witness take the declaration, if he would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljuic. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, towards the end of the day, Mr. Nice informed us that we would be receiving some documents with what he called alleged or, rather, alleged intercepts. However, I have received none of that, and this morning I see two binders placed here on my table. I don't know what they contain, along with the explanation that we were served that last Friday, whereas we were served nothing last Friday. So as far as I'm concerned, these are completely new documents. And last time, the practice was that when we had a witness here, Mr. Zoran Lilic, that half an hour before the end of the cross-examination prior to that day, on the eve of that day, we received two binders. On that occasion I succeeded in reading through them all. However, the ones I've been served this morning, there is absolutely no theoretical possibility of my reading through them, and I don't think they could be introduced in similar fashion, and please would you stop this kind of practice. It would be common decency before a witness comes in that I'm given the documents relating to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The sensible course may be this: That the evidence in chief, direct evidence, should be given; we will then consider the position about cross-examination. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there should be no problem with this witness. As I explained yesterday, the materials were all provided to the accused and his associates last week, I think electronically, which is acceptable to them, and we then -- and that included the transcripts of the intercepts. We then identified yesterday the material that was going to be relied on at a maximum, and therefore, it was open to the accused or his associates simply to find the material from the material that they'd already been provided last week because it was fully identified. I'm happy to tell the Chamber that in the event even of the very reduced binder of exhibits before you, many -- or even in the reduced binder of exhibits before you many exhibits are not going to be produced, so it's going to be smaller in number. And as to the intercepts, we may seek to play one or two of them, but as the Chamber knows, the intercepts, when produced, really are produced, first of all, subject to later arguments that have to take place, and they're produced for purposes of authentication because usually, sometimes the odd one will be played on the basis that there will be a more comprehensive exercise in reviewing and analysing the intercepts if and when they're formally admitted at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you could clarify --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that all the materials are provided to the accused and his associates last week electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, CD-ROM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it in files --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was provided in a CD, and this is happening on a regular basis that material is provided to them electronically, and they're entirely happy for that. In fact, it's preferable, I think. And it's provided in Word, the language Word, with Zy-find as a search engine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it proposed that this witness should produce this bundle of -- what are there here -- 36 intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Produce them in the sense that, as you will have seen or be able to see from the schedule, he can identify the voices on them, and that's something that has to be done at some stage. Produce them in the sense of going through all of them; no, because once they are identified, they can then be put back, for the most part, to the exercise that comes later of authenticating by proving the origins of the intercepts and then dealt with along with all intercepts in a comprehensive exercise of analysis at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But will there be a witness who the accused can cross-examine about them if he wishes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As he has done with other tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. He can cross-examine this witness about these intercepts, if he wishes. He was notified last night which particular ones were going to be relied on and he was provided them, as I say, electronically last week. But, yes, there will be another witness who will give context, we hope, for all intercepts at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The sensible course would be to hear the evidence and see what to do at the end of the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what I've said is that we will rule at the end. When we've heard what this witness has got to say, we will rule at the end about cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, I would like -- all I'd like is to state once again that I did not receive the documents in -- or, rather, information in any form, either in paper form or electronically. Secondly, a moment ago Mr. Nice said that this witness will be called upon to identify voices. I don't know how this witness can identify voices --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. Just wait a moment. We're going to hear it. We're not going to hear it at the moment. We're going to hear it in the evidence as to how he can. Now, if there's an objection, we'll hear it, but there is no question of dealing with that now. As I've said, if you're in any way prejudiced about cross-examination, we will consider that and we'll consider the right course to take. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I should like to draw your attention to the fact, Mr. May, that here, if nothing else, then at least to the papers given to us yesterday by Mr. Nice, where there is a table and review of some conversations. And take a look at what it says. For example, 8th of June 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to. I've explained. We're going to start his evidence. If you have an objection to a part of it, you can do it when we come to it. But in the meanwhile, we're going to hear the evidence, and as I say, if you're prejudiced in cross-examination, we'll consider what to do next. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, as a member of HDZ, which you joined in 1990, did you become president of HDZ Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb in September 1990, and at a convention in April 1991, were you re-elected as president, serving thereafter as member of the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, subsequently the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from November 1990 until November 1992, and then later from October 1993 and until 1996?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The transcript has that he was a member of Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you elected as a member -- were you subsequent -- were you a member of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the first democratic elections in 1990, I was elected with relatively the highest number of votes to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Kljuic, if my analysis of your history is correct, subject to that one correction by the deletion of the word "Serb," if the history is correct, just say so, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. In the first sentence, it says that I was elected in Zagreb for president of the HDZ. That's not correct. I was elected on the 7th of September, 1990, in Sarajevo. And on the 23rd of April, 1991, I received the HDZ convention in Mostar. So I wasn't elected in Zagreb but, rather, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. There was a misprint there. Very well, let's move on to paragraph 6 to 8 very briefly. Were you a member of the Commission for Protection of Constitutional Order?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 8. Did Mrs. Plavsic play a role in this commission?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: She was the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive bulletins by way of information in your work on that commission?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mrs. Plavsic also receive those bulletins, but did she, in your judgement, do something to counter the information of one kind or another that was coming in via those bulletins?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The lady received the bulletins, and in the first stage of work everything was aboveboard and in order. However, as the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia became more complicated, there was manipulation and abuse of the position of president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at simply one example of the material coming your way, if we may.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 15 in a binder of exhibits that I would ask be given a single exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 503.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll just look at this one tab. In the English version, it's at page 5 of 44, and it has you, Mr. Kljuic, speaking. In the B/C/S version, it is at a page at the top numbered T1/7 and onwards. And there is included in that a passage, first of all, where you're intervening and saying that the press mentions your name a lot, and then in the next entry it says: "It's also in today's newspapers." But then it goes on a little later - and this is on our page 6 - to Alija Delimustafic takes over, and over at our page 7 of 44, which would be in the B/C/S at, I think, your page 10, Mr. Kljuic, you see there is reference, page 7 of 44, to this, it says, "Next -- Skrba," and that is on your page 10, "Kujacic, Veselinovic, Bata on barricades - the worst four criminals on one side." And then it goes on throughout that next page to deal with crimes and indeed to deal with, as we can see on the top of our page 8 of 44, reference to Arkan's. Now, we don't want to take the Chamber's time beyond just seeing the generality of what's contained there. Did these reports coming in to the Council of Protection of Constitutional Order contain a review of what was happening on the ground including criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I said that in the first stage, the reports were very proper, but as the situation became more complicated, there was abuse. Now, when I asked that Mrs. Plavsic and Zepinic distance themselves from the barricades, it was clear that on the one hand they represented members of the state commission for security and that they were deeply involved in the erection of the barricades. It would be very important had they said, "No, we don't need any barricades and we haven't got anything to do with the barricades," but they couldn't say that because they would lose face in the political positions they occupied. So it was impossible to be both a member of the security service for the state while at the same time supporting the creation of the barricades and general chaos in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraphs 10 and 11, Your Honours, would lead to production of Exhibits 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Time is at a premium, I will review the need to put those in when I conclude the rest of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I move to paragraph 12. Did you have regular contacts with ex-President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The well-known Karadjordjevo meeting, did Tudjman ever tell you or hint anything to you about the content of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. Actually, as an HDZ leader for Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was seen as a Bosnian patriot and integralist of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I did not accept the idea on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina at all. However, without the disclosing the source of the conversation, President Tudjman told me on one occasion that he had been given from Mr. Milosevic Cazin Krajina, which is the north-western region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, inhabited mostly by Muslims. And I said, "Mr. President, it's the same as if I were to give you as a gift Sardinia or Sicily, for example, because it doesn't belong to you and it doesn't belong to Mr. Milosevic." Cazin Krajina, that is. Of course, as the ideas about a division for Bosnia-Herzegovina were advocated at different levels and from different protagonists, our mutual clash about this idea, that is to say the division of my homeland, gave rise ultimately to the fact that we severed relations, and if you like my elimination from the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina precisely at the time when I was supposed to be president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we clarify the record? The area is Cazin Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or Bihac Krajina, whichever you prefer. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The other point -- now I may have misheard this; that President Tudjman, if we look at the -- if you would look at the line as it's recorded: "President Tudjman had told me on one occasion that he had been given Cazin Krajina, which is inhabited mostly by Muslims." I thought that the witness said, and I may be wrong about this, that it was Mr. Milosevic who had given Tudjman Cazin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain the position, please, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As to what Mr. Tudjman said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President Tudjman said that from -- he had been given Cazin Krajina from Mr. Milosevic, and that is why my reaction was that it would be tantamount to being given Sardinia, because it's a territory that doesn't belong to either Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In early 1991, did to your knowledge Izetbegovic and Milosevic have talks on the topics of the Muslims staying in the Rump Yugoslavia? If so, to what effect?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course on several occasions negotiations were conducted between different parties and also between Belgrade and Mr. Izetbegovic by the same token. At that time, Belgrade endeavoured at all cost to attract the Muslims for this Rump Yugoslavia. They claimed, among other things, that they would be the second nation or ethnic group in a state of that kind. And when they weren't successful with Izetbegovic, then a so-called historical agreement was made up, signed by the other Muslim politician, the one who did not have the support of the people, and his name was Adil Zulfikarpasic. Now, that historical agreement was supposed to separate the joint struggle of the Croats and Muslims on one side, and they did not want to have it waged through the institutions of the system, that is to say through the Presidency, Assembly, and government as legal bodies, but they wanted to sidestep the system and go beyond it. And with a group of Muslims who did not have any -- the support or enjoyed the respect of the population. In fact, this was a trick, and had it succeeded, the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have been faced with a fait accompli or they would be told to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. If they stayed, they would not be equal, an equal ethnic group. If they left, they would get minor territories in Western Herzegovina, which were always mentioned when the question of the Croat secession arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In this particular setting, did you speak to Izetbegovic on one particular occasion about this? And if so, tell us what his reply was.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, it was improper on Izetbegovic's part for not having told me that he had conducted talks of that kind in the first place. And secondly, when I learnt through my own channels about this, I said quite openly -- actually, they had proposed that he be president of the Assembly of that future Yugoslavia. And then I said to him, "All right. If you stay in Yugoslavia, you will be the number two nation or ethnic group in that community. And who is the second ethnic group in Serbia today?" And his answer was, "The Albanians." So I said, "So they're offering you the position the Albanians hold there." But Izetbegovic said at the end, "Stjepan, nothing will come of it."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on then to early July of 1991 or, actually, June of 1991. Was there a session of the Krajina parliament, as it was known, held in Bosanska Grahovo on the 27th of June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. That is the day of the uprising -- no. I'm sorry. Did you say June or July? I didn't quite hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I said June.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: June. In those days, the Serbian Krajina had already been formed in Croatia, and the Bosnian Serbs were endeavouring to form their own autonomous regions, SAOs, and to one day unite territories in the Republic of Croatia with territories in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at the session of this Krajina parliament, was there a declaration to that effect?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did issue a declaration on the unification of those two Krajinas as the first stage in the unification of all Serbian lands. However, such a unification meant undermining the sovereignty of the two republics and was contrary to the constitutions of both the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In your judgement, does that declaration and the policy behind it fit with or explain Karadzic's view on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina otherwise being pursued?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That was certainly part of a global policy of unification of all Serbs, so that they would all live in one state, and that idea was in direct contradiction with the existing situation, and in the final analysis, it was in contradiction with the Helsinki conference, the decisions of which would later on have a decisive impact on the future of my homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 16. In the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did the SDA propose that the act of unifying the Krajinas constituted a violation of the constitutional order of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. And not just the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The vote on that proposal led to what, so far as the SDS deputies are concerned?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Our parliament, at a regular sitting, condemned this act and felt that this was an act destroying the territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Finally, the SDS deputies walked out of the parliament sitting, which they often did so as to disavow the Assembly. And -- however, we could always continue working because we had the necessary majority. But in fact, when decisions were taken, we really wanted representatives of the Serb people to be present because the SDS had won the majority of the Serb vote, though there were some Serb representatives from other political parties present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 17. In September of 1991, did you meet President Tudjman in Zagreb where he suggested that you should have talks with the SDS? Did you return to Sarajevo and contact Karadzic the next morning? If so, did he seem surprised by your call or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I frequently had meetings with President Tudjman, but at a certain point in time during my visit to Zagreb, he insisted that I also negotiate with the SDS. Actually, I had talked to Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Koljevic earlier on, as well as with Mrs. Plavsic. However, they didn't want Bosnia-Herzegovina under any circumstances. And also, they didn't recognise the Republic of Croatia. In that context, they kept criticising me and accusing me of being loyal to Izetbegovic. And this was very successful as propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know it's temptation, but --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was successful propaganda. However, precisely because of that propaganda, President Tudjman said, "Stjepan, you can't just talk to the Muslims. Have you to talk to the Serbs as well very seriously." And when I reached Sarajevo in the morning, I called Karadzic by phone, however he wasn't surprised. It could be assumed that Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic had been in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 18. Later in September 1991, did you and Stanic meet with Krajisnik, Karadzic and Koljevic, and did it seem to you that the Serb representatives wanted to gain Bosnian Croat support?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course everyone was looking for allies, and they worked in parallel primarily with Izetbegovic because that would mean most of the job done, but obviously there were also suggestions that we should talk amongst ourselves. Stanic and I visited the Serbian delegation consisting of Krajisnik, Karadzic and Koljevic, and that was the time when the war was already raging in Croatia. As Tudjman insisted that I talk to them, I simply put them to the test and said roughly, "My people would kill me if they knew that I was sitting at the same table as they when Croatia was burning. However, we are politicians, and we have to talk." I said that a gesture on their part would strengthen my political standing and that by doing so, they would confirm the sincerity of their wish for cooperation. I simply asked of them that they recognise the Republic of Croatia within its Avnoj borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Their reaction to that, in a sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Dreadful. They said that they would never accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And did that lead really to the distancing of you from the Serbs, they being keener on finding another Croat with whom they might cooperate?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. No. They knew that they couldn't make a deal with me against Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, as the situation became more complicated in Bosnia, within the framework of the HDZ there was a pro-Serb lobby with which they started to cooperate. And when the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina took place, that cooperation at times reached optimal levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you report back to President Tudjman on the reaction of the SDS leadership and its non-acceptance of the Republic of Croatia and its borders?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what was President Tudjman's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: His reaction was also dreadful. Maybe he realised just then that what he was advocating at a higher level had still not even reached the Bosnian Serbs as a piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 20. On the 22nd of January of 1991, had you attended talks in Belgrade? The Bosnian delegation including Izetbegovic, Koljevic, and yourself; the Serbian side including the accused, Trifunovic, and a third person whose name is misspelled in the summary, I think. Who was the third person?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Unkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Unkovic. I'm not particularly troubled by the meeting itself save to say this: Did the meeting end with -- the formal part of the meeting end, paragraph 21, with an agreement that their future Yugoslavia would be a joint democratic country of equal peoples and republics?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I have to say two sentences by way of introduction. Mr. Milosevic, in October 1998 at a Central Committee meeting of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia declared that Serbia was not interested in the territories of other republics, and for us, this was one of the arguments we used at the negotiations held on the 22nd of January, 1991. So in Bosnia, the elections were completed in November, in Serbia in December, and we immediately hastened to meet with the Serbian delegation in order to reinforce the principles of the future Yugoslavia, and those were primarily the equality of the republics. And that is why I was pleased and satisfied with this meeting held on the 22nd of January in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After the meeting and at lunch, did the accused take you aside and have a private conversation with you? Paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I have to say that Mr. Milosevic showed a high degree of hospitality towards me and even some friendly feelings, and we got up from the table and he said to me that he understood the wishes of the people of Western Herzegovina to join Croatia. But this was a repeated trick used by the Serbian side whereby a smaller segment of the Croatian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be allowed to unite with Croatia, and for us this had enormous consequences, because unfortunately, that portion of our people believe to this day that they could be attached to Croatia. However, I said to him that we -- there was a misunderstanding between us as to what Western Herzegovina is, and I must admit that with a high degree of precision, Mr. Milosevic said half of Mostar, 70 per cent of Capljina, Ljubuski, Posusje, Grude, Tomislavgrad, Citluk, Siroki Brijeg, 70 per cent of Livno, and with a smile he said the whole of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: And Prozor was interesting because --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pausing there, we'll come back to Prozor in a second, but you've remarked on the detail with which he made this offer. Have you represented on a map which will now be produced, Exhibit 34 -- 343, tab 5, now marked by the witness and perhaps can be shown on the overhead projector. This, Mr. Kljuic, is the map you've marked I think yourself to reflect what it was the --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't see the map, but there's no problem, I know exactly what I marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see it on the left-hand side. It's not showing up on my screen either. Go back to Prozor and use the pointer just to explain anything you want to. The usher will hand you the pointer.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I think there was a rather charming sentence uttered: "We'll give you the whole of Prozor in Herzegovina too," because you must know that Prozor was a municipality in which there were no Serbs. There was a Serb policeman once for three years. He couldn't find a wife, and he left. So it was a compact community of Muslims and Croats of Bosnia. But I said that we didn't agree as to what Western Herzegovina was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So your reaction to his proposal -- or do you want to explain more your understanding of what Western Herzegovina was? This was his proposal. What would your understanding of Western Herzegovina have been?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I meant a far broader territory, but that isn't important for this case. What is important is that I said to Mr. Milosevic, "So the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be yours, would it?" And he was a charming and charismatic man who smiled a lot. Just then, I used -- I resorted to some Bosnian humour and showed him the Bosnian coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's probably not a detail we need to go into in this court, I think. So we'll go to paragraph 23 instead. The meeting of the Presidency in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of December, 1991, was one where there were two points on the agenda. The first was re-election of the president, and following various complexities was Izetbegovic re-elected? And I don't want an account of the complexities.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: According to the constitution, Izetbegovic was entitled to continue being the president of the Presidency for another year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. If the accused or the Chamber needs the detail, we can have it, but I think it's sufficient to say that he was re-elected, for our purposes. So we move on to the second item on the agenda, which had to do with the European Union's request that Bosnia-Herzegovina finalise its request for independence. How did support for that proposal manifest itself on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, it was clear that Yugoslavia could no longer prevail. The horrors of the war in Croatia led Slovenia and Croatia to take the final decision to leave Yugoslavia. They also had declarations of independence and a referendum, and in such a Yugoslavia the Muslims and Croats of Bosnia did not wish to remain. So we --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Time is short. I hope we are over halfway through your evidence-in-chief. Can you just tell us, please, what happened in the Presidency. How were the votes cast on this particular issue on that day?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Five members of the Presidency voted in favour of independence and a referendum, whereas Koljevic and Plavsic were against it. And from then on they froze their status, which meant that sometimes they came, sometimes they didn't come to attend, depending on their interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then paragraph 25. The conclusion to seek independence was something that then had to be dealt with by the Assembly. In the Assembly, was Krajisnik and the Serb bloc for or against independence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: They left the Assembly meeting. First of all, Krajisnik obstructed the proceedings with various discussions. He tired us out. And at 5.30 -- no, at 3.30 in the morning, he walked out of the Assembly. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. However, an absolute majority of members of the Assembly remained, among whom there were some Serb deputies from the Communist Party, the reformists, and some other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These votes and the decisions taken, in your judgement, mark the start of the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 29. I pass over the control of the Assembly simply to this: Did presidents of parliamentary parties have the right to come to Assembly meetings? Did Karadzic do that from time to time, and did he make a speech about the effect of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The presidents did have that right. The presidents of the parties in power could be given the floor out of order. Karadzic availed himself of this right and made his well-known speech when he said, "If you insist on independence and prevail, there will be no Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Muslim people will disappear."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 8 of Exhibit 503, please. If you'd be good enough just to look at that. To mark their attitude or their separate attitude from that of the rest of the Presidency, did Plavsic and Koljevic write a letter on the 16th of September of 1991 support to the Federal Secretary of National Defence of the army, Vjelko Kadijevic, dealing with the decisions passed by organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina relating to a unified system of defence being passed by outvoting the legitimate representatives of the Serbian people in these bodies. "In this way, the public is being given a distorted image of the attitude of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the army and the defence of the country. "It is, however, true that the entire Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as most patriots and pro-Yugoslavs of other peoples are faithful to the idea of preserving Yugoslavia and the army as the only guarantee of civil peace and safety. "The presence of the JNA ... is a firm guarantee against the actions of other illegal armed formations." And then ending - I miss out a few passages - "... in the name of the Serbian people and all the peaceful citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we fully support the unified armed forces of Yugoslavia in the execution of their constitutionally defined roles and tasks." In your judgement, was that letter one that demonstrated the distance between the Serbs and the rest of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The letter is authentic. However, the information it contains is false, namely in those days because of the dreadful war in Croatia and the misdeeds committed by reserve units of the JNA in Bosnia, there were fewer and fewer people supporting the army, because in the first place, it had become a single nation army, and in all disputes it always sided with the Serbs. Therefore, the army no longer enjoyed the support of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and many wanted the army to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina as soon as possible, even though we in the Presidency had promised long since that the part of the army stationed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, once we get independence, we would accept them as our own army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 31. Was the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina swelled by troops withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia along with reservists from Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. In those days Bosnia was the largest barracks in the world, because all the units that had been pulled out from Slovenia and Croatia came to Bosnia, and particularly various corps from Titovo, Uzice, Valjevo, Podgorica and others, from Serbia and Montenegro, even though Serbia and Montenegro were not in jeopardy at all. So Bosnia and Herzegovina had a very high concentration of the military, many of whom belonged to forces outside Bosnia and Herzegovina, or units outside Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the Presidency send a delegation to Belgrade to come to an agreement with Kadijevic about the withdrawal of troops from Bosnia and about those that could remain in Bosnia and be supported there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: We really had a very clean-cut political position, that in the process of secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina we should take over all the regular troops belonging to Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, we were against the arrival of other JNA units coming. And in those days already, parents would not allow their sons to be recruited to the JNA. So we tried to talk legally, and we sent a high-level delegation to Belgrade, however, except for a few customary phrases, these talks bore no fruit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 24th of December of 1991, was there a meeting between the Presidency and JNA generals led by Kadijevic, all participants except Admiral Brovet being either Serbs or Montenegrins?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Brovet was an admiral.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the end of the meeting - and I only want this - did Izetbegovic -- or at some stage in the meeting did Izetbegovic speak to General Kadijevic about paramilitaries who were active in Bosnia; and if so, what did Kadijevic say?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Kadijevic clearly took Serb positions and said, "You take care of the political side and I'll take care of the military side." Let me explain what that meant. What it meant was, you stay in Yugoslavia and then the army will not touch you. However, Izetbegovic, even if he had wanted to, would not have been able to put into practice a policy of this kind. And he did not want to do so, in fact, because the citizens in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the population - and I should like to stress in particular a significant proportion of Serbs living in urban areas especially - were opposed to what the army was doing in Croatia, and that that is true we would see later on, because the percentage of the -- the percentage of the population who voted at the referendum for Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just give me one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 34. From late 1991, Mr. Kljuic, did you become aware from various reports of military activity around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Namely what? What was being reported?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: You would have to know that at that time, there was democratic power for the first time, civilian power apart from the army. And that was different from the communist regime where the army and the party were united. And so we wanted to receive information as to the army's movements on the ground. Although that was our constitutional right, in fact, it took a long time for us to be able to get that information. And the army kept bringing in information, sending in information, saying that they were going to do training in the outskirts of town. However, our observers and the Defence Ministry as well but the citizens too, noticed that what they were in fact doing were making an encirclement around the town and building fortifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Were barricades erected by both Bosnian Serbs and then by Muslims in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: As we held a referendum on independence, Karadzic at all cost wanted to prevent international recognition for us, because in his view, numerous preparations had been undertaken in the blockade of Sarajevo itself. He organised the barricades to test and see how far the city was prepared to resist those barricades. And it was especially important in the centre of town, in a place called Pofalici, which allows for the possibility of Sarajevo being divided in two, split into two parts. And when the barricades were erected, it was found that the Serb paramilitary forces could not divide up Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I think you moved your belongings to the Presidency and lived there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the war and the aggression, I lived in the Presidency building. But before that, I had to come in there because parts of Sarajevo were blocked, and I live near the airport. And I wasn't even able to go to work for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how long did you stay living in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I lived in the Presidency until October 1992. And once I was eliminated from the Presidency, I had to move out, move out of my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time, was the JNA holding itself out as neutral vis-a-vis the international community?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, no. It wanted to be, or, rather, absolutely, but it was deeply involved. It armed the people, gave them logistic support, and when they were in an inferior position, the JNA would come in to set up an alleged buffer zone to separate us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of the presence of a group called White Eagles, or Seselj's men; and if so, what did you see them doing or what did you discover them to be doing?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The first time during the barricades in March, the paramilitaries from Serbia turned up too, amongst whom were the most aggressive, Arkan's men and Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Seselj's men, Seselj's paramilitaries, had some sort of white band around their heads, and they were well-known by their brutality and also for the looting they did of material goods. And we can say quite frankly that they differed in that respect from the other formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there forces from Nis of which you were aware? Paragraph 35, I think.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the former Yugoslavia, the Nis Specials were considered to be the elitist -- elite commandos, and they were in Sarajevo at a number of locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: During the month of May, was there shelling on Sarajevo? If so, was it particularly heavy on certain days? Paragraph 37.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The shelling was continuous. However, real hell broke out with the arrival of Ratko Mladic, who organised the strongest shelling. And particularly difficult were the days of the 14th, 27th, and 28th of May, and 29th of May too, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that month - paragraph 38 - did you participate in meetings with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: We wanted the army to leave Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina generally. And within the frameworks of cooperation with UNPROFOR, regular meetings were held which had as their goal to determine the conditions under which the army could leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Bosnian negotiators were yourself with Abdic and Doko, Pusina and Siber?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic, Doko, yes. Pusina and Siber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Serbian side was represented by?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic, General Tolimir, Colonel Cadjo always, and then the others would change and rotate, generals who came from Belgrade, such as Aksentijevic, Stojkovic and Boskovic, and some other officers of a lower rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the JNA wish to take their weapons with them when they left? Were they allowed to do so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It did want to take the weapons with it, but we didn't agree to that. And then, allegedly to save face for the Serb soldiers, they had to have their own sidearms, carry their own sidearms. However, when the evacuation actually came about, they didn't take anything with them. But beforehand, they had made all the heavy weapons that were in the barracks inoperational.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 18, please. The agreement, or one of the agreements dealing with the removal of commands, units, and institutions from garrisons in Sarajevo. It sets out the parties and sets out in Article 1 how the parties agreed that the JNA would return armaments, ammunitions, mines and so on, which had been entrusted to it. Article 2, within the framework of the withdrawal of the JNA from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, withdrawal of commands, units and institutions with armament, ammunition, mines, and explosives, equipment, removable property which remains after restoring what belongs to the Territorial Defence from certain garrisons. Is this the agreement that was made, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but it was never put into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us about Pofalici being the critical place for the division of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had the town been split around that point, what would have been the consequences for the old part of Sarajevo? Paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, it wouldn't have been able to survive the siege as the town of Sarajevo had done for 44 months. It could probably have taken it for 15 or 20 days, but then either the population would have started to -- dying of hunger and thirst, or the aggressor forces who were militarily superior would have entered the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I conclude this topic, can we divert to intercepts that you have reviewed generally. Mr. Kljuic, have you, while here in The Hague, listened to several or indeed really quite a large number of intercepts for the purpose of identifying speakers where you can?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 2 of Exhibit 503 is not the draft version provided yesterday but the final version that's been signed by the witness, as the Chamber will see on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Many of these are marked, on the exhibit that you've signed, as being between Karadzic and Milosevic. What opportunities did you have to know the voices of those men? Put shortly and in light of the observation that the accused made this morning: How were you able to identify the voices?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, I had known Karadzic for 30 years, and I think that even before politics, I had contacts with him. And Mr. Milosevic has a characteristic voice. I listened to him for many years over television, so I can say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Other names are shown in the left-hand column of this exhibit, including such names as Koljevic, Jovic, Branko Kostic, and so on. Were these voices you were able to recognise because you have met the people personally or were they voices you identified because you'd heard them on the television - we see Seselj's name there - or was it sometimes one, sometimes the other, sometimes both?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First, let me say that I was able to establish only those things that I was certain of, and I certainly recognised Mandic's, Koljevic, Josic, Kostic, and Karadzic's voices, Milosevic's, the voice of Biljana Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Plavsic because I had contacts with most of those people. And it's very easy to recognise Kostic because he speaks the Ijkavian dialect with the Montenegrin accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same exhibit has on the right-hand side comments. Sometimes the comment is simply a summary of what's being discussed. For example, number 3 simply speaks of Milan Martic causing them problems. Sometimes the comments go a little further and set the transcript into a context. Are those comments your comments, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if -- you said that this witness listened to these intercepts for the purpose of identifying the voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why did he make such extensive comments on each of these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To assist. Possibly it becomes helpful to give evidence about it, but certainly to assist so that the intercepts can immediately be seen in the setting, so that if the accused or anybody else wants to ask about them, they can know what they amount to. I'm certainly going to ask him, as the summary reveals at paragraph 13, whether we should listen to number 35 on the list. I think that might be quite helpful at this particular stage. And what we've done with these intercepts is the same as was done with Dr. Williams a couple of weeks ago, where exhibits were produced and his comments were placed on the right-hand side, it being a helpful way, it seemed to us, to provide material to the Chamber. And provided in advance yesterday, I think probably in a longer format yesterday because I've reduced the commentary to make the document shorter. With the Chamber's leave, may we count as produced to the extent consistent with our practice in respect of intercepts, these intercepts because the witness can identify the voices. They are, of course, produced as transcripts in a separate binder, as the Chamber will have seen, but if we can deal with them on that basis, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can deal with them on this basis: They can be marked for identification. They cannot yet be admitted because the evidence to admit them has not been given on which such a ruling can be based, but they can be marked for identification. But before we get there, I'm not -- I'm also concerned about the status of these comments. I don't think we can admit the comments in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that -- well, first of all, the exhibit generally is being admitted for identification only. That will apply to tab 2 itself. The alternatives are, I suppose, as follows; to leave the comments there but not to count them as in any sense being exhibited, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That might be a sensible solution. If you want to rely on any of them, then of course the evidence had better be given live so it could be challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. But I'm very concerned to take as little time as possible, ensuring that the witness has done the exercise that has to be done by someone, which is to identify the voices. But can we therefore certainly just listen to number 35, which Ms. Wee is in a position, I think, to play for us straight away once we've found it, or have it played it straight away, once we find it in the binder. [Audiotape played]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello? "Good morning."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're getting no English. I don't know what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that number 35 does not correspond to the tape we were hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I had wondered that all along. I have 35, conversation between Abdic and Mladic. Is that what we're supposed to be hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a minute. Yes, it does become Mladic later on. If you turn over the page. It's unidentified to begin with. We have to go on a little bit further before we get to Mladic at about page 3 of 6, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, why are we playing this one in particular? Can you just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It relates to what the witness has just been saying about the shelling of Sarajevo and the change when Mladic came on the scene.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they heard a portion related to the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is obviously a shortcoming in the presentation of that tape. May I come back to that after the break when I've tidied matters up. Your Honour, I certainly would, in an ideal world, like to take one or two more of these tapes or the transcripts from them, but again, I'll decide on that, if I may, after the break and move on to try and see what else I can cover before the break, I having already been one hour and, I think, ten minutes in evidence. If we move on to page 11 of the summary, paragraph 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In April of 1992, did the Presidency form a delegation to see what had been happening in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you go yourself or did you hear from others of what they found?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, but the Defence Minister, Jerko Doko went, and he told me what he had experienced over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what did he experience, according to what he said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, we have to place Bijeljina within the context of the general situation. The first crime in Bosnia-Herzegovina was committed by the JNA troops in the Croatian village of Ravno. However, neither the public nor the SDA attached sufficient solidarity with the casualties, and the JNA did not wish to allow a state delegation even to conduct an investigation into the crime carried out in Ravno. However, when the crime took -- in Bijeljina took place, then the SDA and the Bosnian public saw this as a shock, and then the delegation, including Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Abdic, members of the Presidency, and Jerko Doko, the Defence Minister, went to pay a visit to Bijeljina. And over there, Arkan was in control, and that was already the well-known footage that we saw when Mrs. Plavsic and Arkan are embracing. But in Bijeljina, there were no consequences on Abdic because we later found that Abdic was their player, and he was the contact man. The only repercussions were with respect to the Defence Minister, who was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to him and what were they forced to do while they were there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Arkan's forces forced him to lie down. Him and his escorts were disarmed while Abdic walked around triumphantly saying, referring to himself as "Babo," and he said, "Nobody will make me lie down." It was clear that Abdic and Mrs. Plavsic had special treatment, preferential treatment in the area. However, once they returned, in their report, Biljana Plavsic said that some young men, burly young men, not paramilitaries or anybody else, any organised force but sporadic young men out of control had killed some Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 46. Did you monitor Abdic's movements and phone conversations in early 1992, fearing that he would flee and leave the Presidency without lawful authority for lack of numbers?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After recognition on the 6th of April of 1992, what did Abdic do and what was the effect of that on the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Abdic was the only person at that time who was able to move around the territories where the Serb forces of the JNA were located, so that he would go to Velika Kladusa and go and come back from Velika Kladusa. But he didn't experience Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state yet. And the story of Abdic's cooperation is a long one, with Belgrade, that is, and Zagreb, his cooperation with them. But later on during the course of events, you'll be able to see this from some of the separate agreements that he reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In any event, did he leave the Presidency in April, leaving the Presidency without a quorum?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He did leave the Presidency a little later on, when we legally replaced Koljevic and Plavsic with those persons who were on the electoral list after them. But Abdic left Sarajevo soon afterwards, and he was working against the legitimate Presidency for -- throughout the time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask one more question at this stage and then review the position over the break, see if there's anything else I really wish to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've spoken on a couple of occasions about the possible separation of Sarajevo, and you've spoken of the shelling of it. As it seemed to you, and you were there, was this likely to have any effect on population movement? If so, how and why?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was calculated that way for many reasons. One of those reasons was that the citizens should bear the brunt of the difficulties they were facing, because the town had no medicines, food, medical supplies. And secondly, there were enormous casualties. On certain days, scores of people were killed and hundreds wounded -- dozens killed and hundreds wounded. Thirdly, any supply routes were blocked, that is bringing in military materiel and equipment too. And finally, during that first stage of the aggression, it was very important for them to block the forces of the Territorial Defence, whereby they were prevented from leaving Sarajevo and to assist some nearby towns at the same time, so that they were taken control of in brutal fashion, they were looted, and afterwards ethnic cleansing was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And had the territorial forces that were blocked been able to move to these other ethnically cleansed towns, might the ethnic cleansing have been reduced or avoided?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Had they been able to leave, they would have prevented many small towns -- they would have prevented the arrival of the JNA and Serb troops to many of the small towns and thereby would have protected the population and prevented ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what, if any, population movement within Sarajevo itself would have followed from efforts to divide it or even to take it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, they tried to pull out some of the Serbs from Sarajevo. And after that, sometimes at the intervention of international observers, permission was given for the elderly, women, children, and the infirm to leave. However, that too was a trick because they fought in quite a different way, that is to say the people defending Sarajevo fought in quite a different way if they had their families in town. So if their families had left town, they tried to follow suit and leave Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, two matters. Firstly, the binder of intercepts. If you want it produced or marked for identification, it should have a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two -- number 2 is the document that serves to identify the speakers, because that's the document -- sorry, tab 2 of Exhibit 503 serves to identify the speakers because that's the document that the witness has signed with the references to the speakers and the identifying marks of the intercept concerned. Might it be possible for the binder to become part of tab 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I just wonder really whether there's any sense in producing it at this stage. You've produced your identifying material. It seems to me that this witness really isn't in a position to produce the binder himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not beyond the level of producing for identification purposes, which is applying to all intercepts at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider the best course to follow. More practically, witness statement -- the statement of the witness B-1010, which was passed to me yesterday, is incomplete. I need a complete copy. And we do need -- if you want to call these people, we must have time to deal with it, if you can find time. If you want to call them next week or whatever time you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very sorry you've been inconvenienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is a matter of time. Mr. Kay, you're here today and tomorrow, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just on the matter of the intercepts, having listened to the argument, it seems to me that really that schedule in tab 2 is as far as it can be taken at this stage, and the binder itself isn't really incorporated into this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And it may be simpler, really, because to try and make it part of tab 2 is going to cause endless problems for those in charge of exhibits. It may be that the right answer is that the witness listens to them, as he has done, and says, "Well, I identify those voices," but that's as far as he can take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that he can't actually produce the intercepts. It may be tidier if that is left to the witness who actually does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I review what we've done with other witnesses to make sure there's consistency. Although I think a witness can produce an object that he can recognise, it's not necessary to go into those sort of byways here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It seems to me the person who made the recording or somebody of that sort is going to be necessary to produce it. Whichever way you intend. We've got intercept witnesses coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I mean, again, not necessarily. If somebody is presented with an object which he or she can recognise, then that in itself can produce the exhibit. So I think it's perfectly possible for a witness to reduce an intercept, to say that, "I've listened to this, it is X and Y speaking," but if we are going to be producing them in any event by another witness, then there is no need to venture down Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these byways of technical admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And also it means that the accused will have the chance of cross-examining somebody else about it rather than what may be a waste of time requiring Mr. Kljuic to come back or something of that sort. Mr. Kljuic, we're going to adjourn now. Twenty minutes. Could you remember, please, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that includes the members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm anxious to get on to cross-examination, and of course time is absolutely of the essence now with every witness. I shan't be, I think at the moment, seeking to produce any more of the documentary exhibits to save time. I shan't seek to replay the audiotape that was either incorrect or wrongly placed. Can I then just return very briefly to tab 2 of Exhibit 503. I would urge the Chamber to admit it as a document inclusive of the comments in the same way as happened with Dr. Williams. The Comments column are exactly the comments of the witness. He signed off on the entire document. They cover various general topics. There's one or two that deal with recognition, but recognition of voices is always resolved in favour of non-recognition. Where he says a voice sounds like Mr. Milosevic but he can't be sure, it's dealt with as Unidentified Male, so that's fine. He deals with comments on himself in, I think, numbers 1 and 7 where he says, I think, the comments are okay or accurate. He sometimes simply summarises what is the -- is on the tape and then sometimes he adds some overall commentary. But they are his remarks. To read out that right-hand column on seven pages I calculate would take about 25 to 30 minutes and I don't want to take that amount of time. If in due course these and all other intercepts are -- and other intercepts are admitted, reviewing them in toto at that time would be quite a major exercise and this witness is in a position to be able to comment on these ones because they relate to matters not only by people he recognises but for the most part on topics with which he is intimately acquainted. Especially where it concerns Sarajevo. So that I ask the Chamber to admit the comments. It may be that the matter won't then be taken further by the accused but it may be that he will, either by reference to the intercepts themselves or by reference to another topic. If he doesn't, then at the end of the trial, any reliance on the comments will of course be subject to the fact that they weren't explored viva voce and that they weren't cross-examined to, but they will nevertheless be available as comments by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying this was done in relation to Dr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't got -- Dr. Williams' paper exhibits. There was a schedule produced with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And with comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, with comments on it, yes. But I really don't -- so that's my invitation to the Chamber. To go through it in detail would take half an hour, and I'd much rather get on with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a very difficult exercise to perform in this way, because in effect we're having comments by the witness put in in a schedule form on material largely with which he was not involved in its creation. Authenticity yet has not been established, and it provides a very great burden on the accused to deal with material in this way. We can just look at the detail of this schedule which may well be open to dispute. It's just this witness's interpretation of recordings that he has heard. Dr. Williams' case was largely different in that he was providing material from documents in a process that he had been involved in and was able to assert what those documents related to in that form. These are detailed comments on conversations, if we look at them, alleged to be between Radovan Karadzic and the accused and other people. It may well -- as well be something that the accused would address you on directly in relation to this material, because I think there's another schedule that's available. I haven't been able to trace it yet, which was a draft form of it which is by no means as certain as to who is the particular parties that are talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not able to accede to this method of proceeding, and I'll explain why in a few words. At the moment, these tapes have not been admitted. It may be in due course they will be, but that will be a matter for us to rule on. The witness is entitled, as he's done, to listen to the tapes and to identify the voices. Those are pure matters of fact. He's entitled to do that, and he can be cross-examined upon it, although it may be more appropriate, if there's a challenge, for that to be dealt with at a later date. But comment upon a tape which nobody's heard, which we don't have the full transcript in front of us, even if the comment is upon something which the witness knows about, and a great deal of it, with respect to the witness, is a running commentary on them which may or may not be admissible in any event. We are, in those circumstances, not prepared to admit the comments. We will admit the summary table as voices identified by the witness, the left-hand column, but the right-hand column we are not prepared to admit. Now, it may be appropriate in due course, once the tapes are admitted and properly proved, if they are properly proved and admitted, it may be proper for Mr. Kljuic to come back and make his comments, but at the moment it would simply not only be untidy, it would be totally incomprehensible to deal with the matter in the way which is proposed. So I think this awaits -- it will await the admission of the tapes. So at this stage we do not admit these tapes. We simply admit the witness's evidence as to the voices which he's heard upon them, and the matter will not be taken any further. It means that the accused will not have to cross-examine upon the tapes. He won't have to. He won't be able to at this stage, although he may, of course, cross-examine as to the recognition of voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Therefore, I won't attempt to ask the witness anything about any of the tapes in those circumstances. Your Honour said that the full transcripts aren't available. If they are required for contextual purposes because of identification issues, they are in fact available in the other binder that we aren't going to produce, but I'm very anxious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be sensible for us to return these binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Either now or at the end of the exercise, it depends what the accused does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll keep them for the moment, yes. There are some documents you referred to as dropping.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we deal with the binder generally at the end of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My calculation is that in fact in evidence there was only about an hour and a quarter, I think, for this witness, and I'd ask that to be reflected because it's -- as you know, my -- I'm sort of a clock watcher now professionally. I have been for a year and four months and I think it's going to go on for a bit. Anything we can do to -- that's all I'll ask the witness for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've heard the discussion about the intercepts. Those are not admitted in evidence now. The only relevant part upon which cross-examination will be permissible at this stage is that part dealing with the voices. If you want to cross-examine the witness about how well -- how he can recognise your voice, you can. If in due course you wish to challenge that the voices are those as alleged, of course you can call evidence about it and we'll consider the position then. It may be at that Mr. Kljuic would have to come back to deal with the matter if there was some dispute. But at the moment you do not have to trouble about that binder that you were complaining about earlier. No evidence was given about it apart from the identification, and that you have notice of in any event. So you should stick to your cross-examination which the Prosecution had an hour and twenty minutes, I would think that that will probably be enough for you too, but in any event, you should stick to the evidence which the witness has given today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. May, I don't see how I can cross-examine this witness in one hour twenty minutes. And secondly -- because that is quite impossible. And secondly, with regard to the intercepts, I wish to repeat my position which hope I made quite clear already on one occasion: That I challenge all the tapes until an expert establishes that they are really authentic conversations. My voice was recorded over a period of 15 years on thousands of occasions, on radio, TV programmes, tape recordings, and any kind of conversation can be fabricated, even a talk with Dali Lama, if you wish. As for the left column and the identification -- every intercept has to be authenticated by an expert that it is really my voice. As for the left column, I will just use the document that we received yesterday from Mr. Nice, yesterday after we adjourned. It is the only document in which there is a column that says "Voice identified." And it says, "Draft version of intercepts for use with the witness Stjepan Kljuic." And then it says, "ID 0524T." You received it at the same time I did yesterday afternoon. So the first says 8th of July 1991, Speaker 1 Karadzic Radovan, Speaker 2 Milosevic Slobodan. And then it says voice identified Karadzic Radovan, and the other person appears to be either a military or political expert from Belgrade. [In English] "Global situation --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, we haven't got this document. The document that we have and the document that has been admitted is in tab 2 of this new binder which is Exhibit 503. Now, that's the document. The document I think you're referring to is a draft which has not been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to assist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some items were dropped from that earlier draft between yesterday and today simply because there were some uncertainties about the voices. They were dropped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the document to comment on, to concentrate on, is that which was in the binder. Now, we've heard what you're saying, and you've heard our ruling. We're not going to admit this binder yet. We're not going to admit these intercepts. But the witness is entitled to say, "I've listened to these voices, I know them, and these are the voices I recognise." Now that's as far as it goes at the moment. Now, if you want more time to cross-examine, now is the time to start cross-examining because if you waste time - you've heard this witness can't be here beyond this afternoon - your time is limited, so don't take it up with argument for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not wish to waste time, but if you say you don't have this document, the column headed "Voice identified" does not exist in tab 2. And here in this column -- I quoted the first intercepts. The second one says, "Cannot tell who is talking to Karadzic," and it says it's Karadzic and me. And then again I cannot identify the other one, it is not Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know what document -- I don't know what document you're referring to. No such --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got tab 2? Why don't you look at the binder and look at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received those tabs, Mr. May, this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, have a look at tab 2, because it's that document which is being admitted, not the one that you were given yesterday. That's the point. So these uncertainties that you're pointing out, not unreasonably, these uncertainties have been removed in the new document, the new version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's obviously quite superfluous for me to waste time on this, but please have a look at the document that I was given yesterday. That's what I received before today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the usher would get it. I think what -- it was the document that we were all given. It's now been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I explain again to assist. The draft document you were provided yesterday came in two parts, slightly differently formatted and it was given in advance in order to assist. It was then put together in a single document in a common format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is confusing, and it's not surprising that the accused has been confused by it. There's a description of the other person appearing to be a military expert and all the rest of it. Well, Mr. Milosevic, all I can say is this, that I'll hand this back to you. It is described as a draft, but it is liable to confuse. The document to concentrate on now is document in tab 2, which doesn't have any of those items in, those vague assertions. Yes. Well, let's begin the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kljuic, you were for a long time at the top echelon of political life of Bosnia and Herzegovina, holding high state and party positions; isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, president of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina, member of the Commission for the Constitutional Order and Security, president and member of the Commission for Establishing War Crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.
