utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you probably held other positions as well. All these important positions that you held, did it require a high level of familiarity with the events that were most turbulent and tragic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, they made for being informed, but during times of high tensions prior to the collapse of Yugoslavia and later on, this was no longer possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kljuic. We will come back to that then later. I see from your statement that you favoured a peaceful settlement to the Yugoslav crisis in one way or another; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, in view of the fact that you had congratulated Herzegovina if it manages to join Croatia by peaceful means, did you see that as a peaceful settlement?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I never congratulated anyone on the annexation of Herzegovina to Croatia. On the contrary, I was -- I supported the integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I thought Herzegovina was a component part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here a document which is a reaction to your congratulatory message. It is B119803. It is your ERN number -- I don't mean yours, I mean the number of the opposing side. And it says: "Sarajevo, the 22nd of January, Socialist Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina sharply criticised the action of member of the Presidency and leader of the HDZ --" "The Socialist Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina today Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sharply criticised the act of member of the Presidency of BH and the leader of the HDZ in BH, Stjepan Kljuic, who was the first to address congratulations to Herzegovina if it succeeds in peacefully joining Croatia. The SDP considers this to be the latest contribution to the trading with peoples and territories." And then it says that, "Kljuic also said that Banovina was the borders of Croatian interest in these areas -- marked the borders, and that it was flirting with those who already see Bosnia-Herzegovina finally divided between two state hegemonies." And then, "This opinion is in accordance with his national headquarters." Do you now remember that event?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: You see, the SDP, or the former Communist Party, was highly critical towards me in view of the fact that I was among the rare people who were not members of the party and yet held high-level positions in the country. These are all insinuations, especially that I go to consult Zagreb before taking a position. I did cooperate with Zagreb, but precisely because I had an opinion of my own. My political career, that part of my political career stopped with the break with Zagreb. However, their criticism is not based on a document from which one could clearly see that I said that. This was a campaign by the Communist Party in an endeavour to put all the nationalist parties in the same heap. It is well known, not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina but far beyond, that I was a consistent supporter of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina and the equality of all three constituent peoples in it, and there are several -- many official documents to corroborate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kljuic. I have here in the tabs given to me earlier on, one is just an extract from a page but it is number A088292, and in the footnote 2 it says: "Those who considered that BH should be divided already at the end of 1991 started the institutional integration of Herceg-Bosnia within Croatia while on the other side advocating public support for the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina while secretly working for its annexation to Croatia." Then there is a quotation: "At the level of diplomacy, our political men in Sarajevo can continue pledging their support for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina as we have been saying so far." This is from the minutes of a meeting between Franjo Tudjman and a delegation of the HDZ of BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. What is the tab number? Can you give us the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was disclosure under Rule 68 of documents linked to Stjepan Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps the Prosecution can find it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "This is confirmed by the testimony of Stjepan Kljuic, who as president of the HDZ was a participant at that meeting." And then you are quoted as saying: "The plan was for us formally to advocate a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas actually they worked quite differently, that is against it, because they didn't want it." Was -- is that an authentic quotation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The quotation may be authentic, but it doesn't apply to me under any circumstances. I think that you too know full well that I truly supported a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is what put me in a position to have to separate from such a policy, and I became a victim of those policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, you also know what you stated on page #, paragraph 4 of your statement: "Milosevic made up a strategy which Mrs. Plavsic accepted quickly." I don't know why you mention her. "The position of the Serbs was that people of all ethnicities had lived well in Yugoslavia and that that was our homeland and that those who wanted independence were destroying the homeland." I advocated Yugoslavia. Wasn't that clear?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I must say that formally you did advocate Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What else was I advocating?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: But in actual fact, in practical terms, you did everything against Yugoslavia. And I can just draw your attention to a few details. First of all, you destroyed the 1974 constitution which was a basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that. There were many witnesses who have spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must allow him to answer. You've asked what else you were advocating. Mr. Kljuic, go on. You say that, first of all, the accused destroyed -- let him finish. Let him finish. Mr. Kljuic, if you can very shortly, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very shortly: I think that our tragedy is that Mr. Milosevic formally advocated Yugoslavia, did everything for Yugoslavia to cease, because in those days few people believed that it was possible for certain republics to secede from Yugoslavia. However, with the subsequent course of events, the aggression against Slovenia and Croatia and the instrumentalisation of the Yugoslav People's Army, the population of the western part of Yugoslavia was resolutely against such a Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kljuic, let's move on. I was quoting your words, actually, where you say that it was the Serb's position that people of all nationalities live well in Yugoslavia, that that was our homeland, and that those who wanted independence destroyed the homeland. And when you say the Serbs, you mean Serbia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. But just a moment. Circumstances changed from the moment that you took over control of the votes in the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Vojvodina, and Kosovo, and then also when you imposed other rigorous things such as the storming of the financial system. And ultimately when you took over the dominant role and influenced the Yugoslav People's Army, which at that point in time was least of all a common army and least of all a Yugoslav army which the events that followed were to bear out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to deal with those marginal things. This storming of the financial system you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Five billion American dollars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Five billion dinars is what the National Bank of Yugoslavia released for the buying up of wheat. And somebody lied to you saying that it was $5 billion. She couldn't have admitted -- the primary issue could not have been $5 billion. But all that was while Yugoslavia existed.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That's how we saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was for buying up wheat and it was $5 billion dinars released by the National Bank of Yugoslavia for the purchase of wheat, so that that was that dramatic entrance, or storming, as you put it, of the financial system, but let's not dwell on that. Now in addition to the functions that we enumerate here, in the course of 1991, you were also president of the Security Council of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also right that this council on the 18th -- I have a note of it here. The 18th of September, 1991, changed its name and became known as the Crisis Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also right -- so we're talking about September; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the 18th of September, 1991, in addition to this decision at the council meeting, and it was still the council, several other conclusions were made and adopted.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Let me hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is this true: That one of the conclusions was the following, that the newly appointed Crisis Staff was duty-bound to lead the whole defence system and to ensure the procurement of weapons. That means we're talking about September 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was to take into account the defence system, but I don't think that it was publicly stated that it should take care of arms and arming, although the people spontaneously began to arm themselves quite seriously based on the experience gained in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll put this document on the ELMO, on the overhead projector, so what you don't believe you can look at, and it is highlighted with a Magic Marker. And it also says to ensure the procurement of weapons; and underneath, it says president of the Crisis Staff, Stjepan Kljuic, and the vice-president, Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The header is the Security Council of the HDZ of BH, and it is on the paper, it is belonging to the organisation, and there is a memorandum at the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is on the papers -- on the paper of the HDZ, but this was done by the technical service because neither my signature is there nor is Boban's. And that is how it is possible that this was compiled in the fashion it was, roughly. But I don't reject the fact that there were many attempts to procure weapons at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you just denied that. But now it says there the procurement of large-scale arms.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This wouldn't have been written officially in this way. It is a document without any signatures. An official document would be given a different form, lent a different form. But the intent was to secure weapons, and you don't have to doubt that because we had already gained previous experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's all I was asking you, but are you challenging the correctness of what is written in that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, this is just not an original document. It is a technical document without any signatures. But the contents are authentic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you say the contents are authentic, then we don't have to confirm it with any signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance, Your Honours. We received this from the OTP, this particular document, and this is just the first page of it. There's just one page. Now, perhaps the OTP could give us an explanation as to why they didn't supply us with the rest of the document, the other pages, which might perhaps have a signature. We just have page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need for them to do that at this moment. Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And by the by, and I assume you can confirm this, that on the 26th of July of that same year - so you're doing this in September - that decisions were taken to proclaim independence in Croatia and Slovenia. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, the declaration on independence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, declaration on independence? Right. Fine. And is it true and correct that at the time when we establish this document was written, on the 18th of September, 1991, that there was not a single clash or conflict anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina during that period, or any incidents breaking out or any intervention by the JNA or anything of the like as you said during today's testimony. Before this, before this question of armaments and the decisions taken at that Security Council of yours.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I'll have to tell you that it would have been too late once the conflict had broken out. The citizens, and especially the functionaries and others followed what was going on at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the time when large-scale troops of the JNA were coming into BH. Reservists were coming in who occupied certain territory and provoked incidents. So it's not true that there weren't any incidents. If you look at the behaviour of the Podgorica Corps in Western Herzegovina, including Stolac, then you'll be able to see that the population was very much afraid of that army. Now, the second thing is the development of events in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Kljuic. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, up until that date, the date on that document that we've just looked at and quoted from, had any incidents broken out in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were minor ones, but not what happened in the second half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said were there any incidents? Was anybody killed, beaten up? What happened? Were there any incidents of that sort in BH?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were. I can't remember the details of some minor incidents, but we were more worried about the grouping of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, but did the JNA intervene at all in BH at that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, but in Ravno it did later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say it didn't. All right, let's move on. Now, are you challenging something that you say in your second statement, page 3, paragraph 7, and I'm quoting you: "We have to remember that that was the time -" and you're talking about October 1991, you can see that from paragraph 6 - "that at the time Bosnia had still not become independent and that the JNA represented a legal armed force of Yugoslavia and Bosnia was technically a part of Yugoslavia. So an armed resistance wasn't a realistic possibility at that point in time." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Milosevic, do you really consider that we as citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina would have to support the illegal behaviour and conduct of the JNA, which had already become highly compromised by that time precisely because it implemented violence over the Croats and Muslims, the population. In October 1992, we gain a very clear picture after the -- what happened in Ravno that the army was an uni-national army, and this was evident later on when top level army delegation came to Sarajevo on the 24th of December for a meeting, and that's why the population feared the army and resisted sending their children to an army of that kind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are both being asked to slow down for the interpreters, and to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you have just mentioned Ravno, in point 3 of your statement, the statement of the 20th, 24th of August, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have a copy of both of his statements, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Which was the passage again? Point 3 of the statement of the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Point 3 of the statement, and it is a statement given on the 20th, 24th, and 26th of August, Mr. Kljuic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "In July and October 1999 I testified under subpoena in open session for the Prosecution in the trial against Dario Kordic." I'm reading that from your statement. It says it was in open session. "During the course of my testimony the Defence did not raise with me either of the issues related to JNA convoys in Central Bosnia, Sarajevo in 1991, or the response of the government to the JNA attack on Ravno. The JNA convoy near Busovaca in 1991 must be viewed in the context of a similar event as it was the stopping of 166 tanks from the 7th to 9th of May 1991 in the village of Prolog near Mostar." Tell me this now, please, Mr. Kljuic: What attack on Ravno are you talking about? What JNA attack on Ravno? When did that JNA attack take place? What attack was it that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The crime perpetrated by the Yugoslav People's Army against Ravno was in the autumn of 1991, and it was the first major incident caused by the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In fact, Ravno is a small Croatian town near Trebinje, and at one point it was on the railway line running from Mostar to Dubrovnik, and the Yugoslav People's Army entered Ravno and killed about ten elderly men and women. And we set up a state commission, a BH state commission in which we had Mr. Ganic, member of the Presidency; government member Mr. Lasic - they were members - and several police, high-ranking officers who were supposed to conduct an investigation into what actually happened in Ravno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's sufficient for the moment. Just -- can you give us the date, please, Mr. Kljuic, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the exact date. I have it noted down at home, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it October of 1992? Is that the rough date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not 1992, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1991. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you have the statement in front of you, Mr. Kljuic, you say later on in paragraph 4, you talk about the convoys, JNA convoys in May and October 1991, and in paragraph 5 you draw the conclusion that during that time, at that time Gojko Susak of Croatia was trying to provoke a conflict with the JNA in Bosnia to divert the JNA away from Croatia in order to give Croatia time to prepare for the inevitable conflict with the JNA. And then you go on to say that the JNA was already looking for justification to use force against civilians on Bosnian territory. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army implemented a programme to take control of the territories which belonged -- which came under the framework of your Ram operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let's leave the Ram operation alone. It didn't exist at all. It was a code name to move to protected conversations, encrypted conversations. So I don't know where you get this Ram, R-A-M, from, but we'll come to that in the course of our cross-examination or, rather during the examination, but you know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I even listened to you speaking about it to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, whether you heard me talking about that or something else, let's leave that alone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I clarify and make matters simpler? The army was supposed to take the lines, take up positions along the lines to which Belgrade had territorial pretensions, along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you know full well that Belgrade didn't have any territorial pretensions whatsoever. I told you that, I told Izetbegovic that when we attended a meeting. You testified here that the conclusion of our meeting was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did -- did the accused -- he's making these assertions and you should have a chance to answer them. Did he say to you at a meeting with Izetbegovic, apparently, that Belgrade had no territorial pretensions? Did he say that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that already in October 1998, [as interpreted] at the central committee meeting of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia he made a statement to that effect, that the 22nd of January, 1991, he confirmed that statement in talking to a delegation from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this -- we were all very happy to hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's move on, Mr. Kljuic, with what you were saying, that Susak endeavoured to provoke a conflict and you did your best to avoid a conflict. And then in paragraph 6 you go on to say that in October 1991, there was another issue involving a convoy, and Zoran Maric, the then-president of Busovaca municipality, spoke to you very briefly, and you said that the JNA would retaliate by sending troops and what would we do then? Or, rather, you asked that they not be blocked. Now, these events, do they not confirm that the JNA never entered into a conflict with the people anywhere, and where bare-handed people stand up to stop the column, you went to intervene there on a number of occasions, and the JNA never resorted to force against people who were blocking the road, although it was able to pass had it used force; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the JNA went to those areas -- their going there was unjustified and they had reinforced their formations and this -- the reaction of the population was one of revolt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're not entering into that. That was up to the JNA. But isn't it clear that the JNA did not use force against these citizens for them to pass through but, as you say in paragraph 4, they spent three days negotiating to have them be given free passage, because they moved around freely, as you yourself confirm, as the sole legal legitimate armed force in Yugoslavia at that time. It was moving around its own territory. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, we can debate point as to whether it was their territory or not and what the role of the JNA was during that period of time. It is true that in the field, on the ground, there were lower-level structures who thought that they could stand up to the Yugoslav army. I personally, and we, all of us together, did not wish to see an incident break out. However, when the units of the Yugoslav People's Army started moving towards all the strategic points which would enable them one day in the future to occupy us, then the people, the populace, was revolted to see this happening. And when 166 tanks moved towards Kupres, advanced towards Kupres, the people spontaneously got together to stop them because the people were afraid of those tanks. And it was my wish to prevent an incident from breaking out, because at that point in time, I myself had been arrested and taken to the air force base in Jasenica where I was told that the JNA had to pass through. And I said how is it going to pass through going across -- through the people? And this resulted in long-winded negotiations and talks, and three days later the tanks were allowed to go through, and I'm very proud to have prevented casualties in an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that and October 1995 where you're talking to Maric, doesn't that precisely deny all assertions that the JNA engaged in violence there? So you spent three days negotiating to let 166 tanks through which did not want to pass through using force. That's quite clear. So that's what you say in your statement. You negotiated for three days.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes, but the citizens did not trust the tanks. They knew it was very strategically important for them for them to park themselves on the elevations above Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I won't belabour the point and waste time on it. All I wanted to establish was that they did not use force. They did not resort to force and you spent three days negotiating to allow the JNA units pass through peacefully.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Milosevic, you know that the army acted outside the agreements of the legal authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't know that they took steps outside any agreement reached by the legal authorities there or anywhere else, because, Mr. Kljuic, as you say yourself, that army was the sole legal armed force during the time, and it was moving around --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm just making sure there's a pause between question and answer. Also, something seems to have gone wrong with the transcript. Apparently it's simply these monitors that have gone wrong and the transcript is running. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Perhaps you could just repeat the question briefly and we'll take the matter up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we really have to hurry, because my time will be interrupted. Is it beyond dispute that the HDZ on the 19th of August, 1990, had a rally in the Sarajevo Skenderija - this is August 1990 - and that the president of the initiating committee, Davor Perinovic, whom you succeeded, isn't that right, addressed the people gathered with the following words: "The enemies of Croats and Muslims are never at rest but our message to them is we won't give Bosnia." The enemies of Croats and Muslims. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite. It was an HDZ convention, and you must be aware of the atmosphere. For the first time after 45 years, the Croatian peoples hymn was played, the Croatian flags were flown. There were many people from abroad present, too. The speech of the president of the initiating committee is not valid, because after all, he was a political amateur in those days, and after we had rid ourselves of the yoke of the communist regime, people gave themselves freedom to express their emotions far more powerfully than was to be expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But isn't it unquestionable that they said the enemies of the Croats and Muslims are never addressed? He never mentions the Serbs, does he? And not only that, but he obviously denotes them as some sort of a common enemy. And this was in August 1990.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: You cannot consider his words as being relevant. Let's not enter into his origins. You know that very well, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kljuic, this was an HDZ convention. Wasn't the message quite clear to the Muslims and the Serbs, one being treated as enemies and the others as friends. And this was in 1990. It is an HDZ rally for Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the first free event, and there was an eruption of emotions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean anti-Serb emotions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, not anti-Serb, anti-communist. However, in this particular statement, that can be said to be true too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm glad you say so. As an intellectual, you respect arguments, there's no doubt about that. So already in 1990, the Serbs were marked as some sort of a common enemy in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Also in the examination-in-chief and on page 5, paragraph 4 of your statement, you say that it was clear that the real intention of the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbs - you probably mean the Serbs of Serbia - to unite Serbia with the Serbian Krajina. You were speaking here about the unification of the Cazin Krajina and SAO Krajina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, SAO Krajina, and the Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The SAO Krajina, but which one?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Glamoc, Drvar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're talking about the Krajina in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember, Mr. Kljuic, that the official position of Serbia then was that this was illegal, that it wasn't serious, and it was unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Correct. I remember that you condemned it but I don't know whether you did so sincerely. They took a step before expectations. That was an amateur step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you remember that that never happened.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was impossible in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when you say that this was some kind of a policy, on the other hand you also are aware of the fact that this was a step that met with a negative response. You yourself say that we condemned such a step.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you must allow, Mr. Milosevic, that it may have been premature. It was due to come later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but those are your assumptions. On page 5, paragraph 5, you say that in July 1991 you were in Zagreb at a meeting with Tudjman who proposed to you that you have talks with the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And upon return to Sarajevo, you called up Karadzic and he told you that he had expected your call.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You then drew the conclusion, because as you say Tudjman and I had a permanent telephone contact between us, that's what you say, so you drew the conclusion that Tudjman told me and I told Karadzic that you would call him.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That was my initial impression, but later, reading Sarinic's book Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about meetings with you, I learnt that you were in contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us not delve into Sarinic's book now. Sarinic will be coming to testify about his book. But did President Tudjman give you any guidelines or suggestions regarding that meeting with representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it logical for him to give you such guidelines if you assume that -- if your assumption about our mutual agreement is correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. I'll tell you why: Because the whole campaign against me - I was obviously in the way of certain elements - was to represent me as a person who had been bought up by the Muslims. Because how come I was not supporting a single Serb position in parliament?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please, as you speak about this, please look at the minutes from a working meeting in the presidential palace. This was a response to Mesic's testimony. I will give you the entire minutes to look at. I will open it on the page which is relevant for this discussion. The president says, President Tudjman: "Everything boils down to the fact that I met with Milosevic 48 times over the division of Bosnia." And then on the next page, it says: "And later on, he admitted that I met him at his proposal. I had two meetings with Milosevic, once with Alija Izetbegovic present. And we said in Geneva or somewhere, we said this together, because these things were being repeated, that we were dividing up Bosnia at that meeting. What we said was that we never discussed the division of Bosnia, but we did talk to Alija in spring 1992. The war in Croatia was stopped, but Alija wanted to remain in Yugoslavia," et cetera. So please look at these minutes. Tudjman is talking to his own associates. These are stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Wait a moment. Now, what is the point here? The witness wasn't there. This is some meeting he will know -- he wasn't present at. Now, what are you trying to achieve, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I wish to challenge the assertion of Mr. Kljuic's, mentioned many times, that apparently Tudjman and I were dividing Bosnia at some sort of a meeting in Karadjordjevo. Tudjman himself denies this among his own associates in 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will be able to bring evidence, if you have any, to that effect. The witness can only say what he saw and heard himself, and that's what he says Tudjman told him. Now, Tudjman may have been saying else to somebody else. We don't know that, we'll have to find out. But the witness can't comment on what occurred at some other meeting. Yes, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, very briefly. First of all, I never said that President Tudjman said he was in Karadjordjevo with Mr. Milosevic. I said that on one occasion he just told me such-and-such a thing about the Cazin Krajina. Secondly, I didn't say I was sure that Milosevic and Tudjman were in touch permanently, but I was surprised by the fact that Karadzic knew I would call him, and he said he was expecting my call. So that was my logical conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I'm sorry if I interrupted you, if there's something important you wish to add, but I wish to draw your attention to paragraph 10 of your statement. You say that in May 1992 -- this is paragraph 10 of your statement: "In May 1992, Boban had a secret meeting with Karadzic in Graz." What have I got to do with a secret meeting between Karadzic and Boban in Graz?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you first that I never claimed this but there was talk about it and Sarinic confirmed this in his book, but let that be a topic to be addressed on another occasion. However, you could have a lot to do with Bosnian Serbs having talks with Croatian representatives. First of all, Mr. Koljevic was with Boras and Manolic, then Mr. Koljevic was in Zagreb seeing Tudjman. They talked about Shakespeare throughout lunch. And this axis Boban-Karadzic was meeting not only when the aggression on Bosnia started but it will be a contact that lasted for a very long time at the expense of my own people, the Serbian people, and at the expense of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think to the detriment of the whole of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that Tudjman told you - which I really don't believe you can remember that, I don't think you're making this up intentionally - that you -- I gave him the Cazin Krajina and you responded it would be the same as if he had given you Sicily or Sardinia, and I quite agree with you. How could I give anyone Cazin Krajina as a present? Don't you remember that one of the leitmotifs that was circulated continuously that Croatia was territorially untenable because it has this crescent form and certain corrections needed to be made in the reconstruction of a future Yugoslavia. That was Zagreb's position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I can't say that it was always the official position, but that such ideas were present in Croatia's policy is beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6, paragraph 5, you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're moving on to something else, we'll stop. But, Mr. Kljuic, let's make sure in case this is challenged. This is what the accused told you about Cazin Krajina; is that right? As I understood your evidence, you had a conversation with him about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. He says that Tudjman told him that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On one occasion President Tudjman said this to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've clarified it. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's quite apparent we can't deal with the 92 bis application today. We'll try and deal with it tomorrow, but since it's your application and your witnesses, you will have to make some time for it. What we can do is deal with it first thing tomorrow morning and try and deal with it orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. I take it from that you were going to allow cross-examination to exhaust today, subject to whatever other examination from the amicus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we have in mind 55 minutes for you, the balance of the afternoon. I'm afraid the amici and re-examination will have to be short accordingly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I absolutely cannot get through the cross-examination of this witness over the next 55 minutes, and could you please bear that in mind. Otherwise, in the meantime, during the break I was given back this piece of paper relating to the conclusions that we commented on, Mr. Kljuic and I, with regards to the procurement of weapons, and I should like this to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be produced. We'll give it the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 163, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, could you please give me short answers for us to save time, because as you can see, my time is extremely limited.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 6, paragraph 5 of your statement you said that the key to the beginning of all the problems in BH was the president's meeting held on the 19th of December, 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that the question of the agenda for the Assembly was the demand by the international community that Bosnia-Herzegovina finalise its calls for independence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I don't suppose you would deny that you were asked to demand independence.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, because that's what we wanted ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "we," do you mean the representatives of just two peoples?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I mean the enormous number of the population which would be borne out by the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Plavsic and Koljevic disagreed with that and left the session?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, they froze their participation in the Presidency meetings.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that act was counter to the constitution. They could either tender in their resignation or be part of the Presidency. They thought up something that was not constitutional, because pursuant to our constitution, if any member of the Presidency should table their resignation, then he would be replaced by the next person on the list, the electoral list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, they did not tender their resignation. And you say on page 7 that it was Plavsic and Koljevic's task to block the Presidency meetings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The interpreters are cautioning me to speak slower because they can't follow at this speed. Now, tell me, how can you speak of their blockade when they froze their positions and work in the Presidency? Didn't they take part at all so how could they have blocked its work?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: In official terms, formally they could not because we had the majority. But as we wanted to arrive at a consensus for the final outcome, it was questionable whether we should respect the elected presidents -- representatives of the Serb people. We wanted them to take part in the work of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you exclude that generally known principle which held true for Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to which decisions must be passed on the basis of a consensus by the representatives of all three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I'm not excluding that. But if BH had an equal treatment with the rest of the Yugoslav republics and if that was offered to all the other republics, and you know about the Badinter Commission, a case in point, and that Montenegro at one point, had it accepted that, then to curtail the rights to BH for independence would have been precisely an infringement of the interests of the citizens of that particular republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And that's why you go on to say that Krajisnik left the Assembly meeting, and you went on to describe that the meeting lasted until 3.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. As I didn't attend the Presidency meeting and you did, could you please confirm or refute the information that I have that Krajisnik, in view of the fact that time was getting on, he said he was interrupting the meeting and that they would continue their deliberations in the morning. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't know if that's what he said, but quite obviously the representatives of the SDS did not want the meeting to come to a conclusion, and as everything was limited by dates and the issues were ones of capital importance, then with the fact that these two people left, they obstructed the calls for independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the fact that this session went on until the early hours of the morning, that is to say from one morning to 3.30 a.m. the next morning -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, with some breaks and interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And is it true that Krajisnik said that as they had been debating for quite a long time and as time was passing, doesn't it seem to be logical to you that he said they would continue the next morning?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there is the senior staff meeting that took the decision. I don't think he promised not to come back. There was no reason not to wait for a few more hours. Quite obviously they had different plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But wait a moment. You that it became clear through that action that they were not in favour of BH's independence.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you not say yourself that they had told you that themselves quite unequivocally? So why did you need to have this sequence of events to understand that, to come to understand that, that they were not in favour of independence for BH?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, this became evident after the lengthy discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they themselves told you that they didn't want independence.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if they said they were not in favour of independence, does that mean that all of us should not call for an independent BH? Should give up our stances?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not telling you what the alternative should be. All I'm saying is that all of you, up until that point in time, and you personally, you who advocated - how shall I put this? - a multi-ethnic principle and approach were in favour of having decisions made by consensus on the part of all three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Of course. But the frameworks of the dependence or independence of BH was normal if you compare it to other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, on page 8, paragraph 1, you say that the basic propaganda of the Serb leadership in BH was that the Muslims and Croats should become armed and that a large number of Mujahedin were ready to come to BH and attack the Serbs there. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is that how it was? Is that what actually happened? Except that they didn't only attack the Serbs, they attacked the Croats too, isn't that right, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't that the Mujahedin at that time were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have to say that the arming of both the Croats and Muslims was child's play compared to what the Serbs had and the JNA with then, which systematically armed the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, we provided a document with respect to armaments, and it dates back to September 1991, and we also have documents testifying to the armament of Muslims also in 1991. So all three parties, all three sides procured weapons. I don't suppose we're challenging that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in a conversation you had with Karadzic, you once said, when he was raising tensions and saying everybody's arming themselves in Bosnia, you said that won't help them. So you, as opposed to Karadzic, were conscious of the fact that all this arming on the part of the Croats and the Muslims, the Bosniaks, was amateurish compared to the military potential of the Yugoslav People's Army and Yugoslavia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you said that there were no Mujahedin. Well, I have here a document, 01099141 is its number, and it provides a list of the Mujahedin -- it is in English -- a list of the Mujahedins imprisoned by the HVO. And then it goes on to list them. There are 11 of them from Algeria, from Tunisia, Pakistan, Egypt, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Turkey.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Possibly, but that was later on, in the later period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in April 1993.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, that is far removed from the period of time we're discussing now and when your propaganda spoke about mass arming on the part of the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, these Mujahedin, did they come because of Serb propaganda or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that period of time because I wasn't a member of the Presidency at that time. I ceased to be it from October 1992 -- or, rather, from 1992 to 1993, October. And that is where that piece of information falls in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about April 1993.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be exhibited, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There's no relevance for it at the moment. The witness has said what he was able to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Now, I have been given by the opposite side over there, Mr. Nice, Mr. May, a -- the transcript -- transcript between Andrew Hogg and Abdul Aziz, a conversation between the two men. It is a translation that I have here, and your ERN number is 03019700, and it speaks about -- or, rather, Hogg is asking him, Can you tell us about the soldiers, the Mujahedin who have come here? And he is asking him whether they are people with combat experience. And he says, Yes; and he says, Where did they get their military experience? And he said, Most of them from Afghanistan but there are some from other countries, and for some of them this is the first time they have been a part of the jihad, and so on and so forth. I don't want to dwell on that. Once again, Aziz responds, and I'm quoting his answer: "The Mujahedin methods, the methods of the jihad are either victory or death to Islam -- death for Islam," which means shadar [phoen], we refer to it as shadar or -- so it's either victory or defeat. Shadar means that we are laying down our lives in the struggle for Islam, and then he asks how shadar is written and he spells shadar for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to stop you but time is limited and there is a limit to what this witness can answer in relation to an intercepted conversation between two other people. Now, he has agreed with you that later on there may have been Mujahedin present. There is no point, it seems to me, to labouring the matter any further. No doubt there are other witnesses or you can call evidence about their presence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among other things, he says that there are many of them. I cannot count them because there are so many of them from every country, and that is what Aziz says, among other things. So this is a document which I was disclosed by Mr. Nice's side, and I'd like to exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There's no reason at the moment to exhibit it. All you can do is to ask the witness what his experience, if any, of the Mujahedin was. You can ask the witness about that, but he can't give general evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the intercepts, however produced, there may be the same problems with authentication. We simply provide the material we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think they are intercepts. This is isn't an intercept, it's an interview between Andrew Hogg, a journalist, and Abdul Aziz. Perhaps Mr. Kljuic can take a look at it and perhaps he has seen this conversation. Perhaps it was published somewhere.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about it. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know how many thousands of Mujahedin there were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedins appeared in 1993, and they inflicted enormous damage to the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's speed the process up. For a time you were president of the Commission for the Establishment of War Crimes in the BH area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you have then, and here before the entire public - and I'm talking about the Croatian public in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, and in Croatia - do you have evidence and information about the crimes and manner in which they were committed and the perpetrators of those crimes? For example, against the Croatian people, for example, in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I have to say that I was president of the commission as a political figure, and the commission was otherwise composed of the leading lawyers of the day, and it was a multinational one, multi-ethnic in composition, and very talented young people who spoke English well and were able to work with computers. The formula as to conducting the work of this kind of commission was given to us by Simon Weisenthal, and the team worked very diligently, objectively, and it recorded each and every event that came to our notice, attended by all the necessary documents if they had them, such as photographic material, videotapes, and the statements of the victims as well, victims to those events. Now, two important inspections were conducted by Mr. Mazowiecki and by Professor Cherif Bassiouni, professor of international law from the University of Illinois in Chicago. They came to inspect our work and they congratulated us on our objectivity and high degree of professionalism on the work of the team, the commission. Unfortunately, once I was eliminated from the Presidency in the fall of 1992 or, rather, October, at the beginning of 1993, I was replaced from my duties there, and I heard that one day over the local radio station. And after me, leading lawyers of all nations as well as the professor of international law stepped down from the commission too, and the most the young experts working on the project. Unfortunately, the commission very soon after that became a one-party and one-nationality, one single ethnic commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you can't tell me even about the crimes committed against the Croats to the best of your knowledge and information.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I can't, because the conflict between the Bosniak Muslims and Bosniak Croats became intensified in 1993, and at that time I myself was no longer in the commission, a member of the commission. But quite certainly the commission does have certain knowledge about those events too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kljuic. Now do you know who Stjepan Siber is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander of the corps, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not the corps but the Territorial Defence to begin with, and later the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. The army of BH. Well, I have a letter here from him and it is titled to the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in person, and the commander of the staff of the Supreme Command of the BH army in person. Addressed to them in person, and among other things, the letter says as follows: It says on the 8th of June, 35 Croats were executed in the village of Bikos and four witnesses were wounded but are still living. And then he says on the 22nd of June, members of the commission for the release of detainees learnt that the Mujahedin one day prior to that near the village of Mehurici shot about 50 civilians under Mount Vlasic, and then mentions 30 more Croats who were shot on the 10th of June, 1993, and then it goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about this. What's the relevance of this? As far as this indictment is concerned, what relevance does it have?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it that the Bosnian Serbs who are responsible for these crimes against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. On the contrary; the Mujahedin are responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And what is the relevance as far as this indictment is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is relevant for the truth, Mr. May. I've told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not an answer. Now, what is the relevance to the indictment, to the events which are covered?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that the indictment is false, and this only corroborates what I'm saying, Mr. May. For you, this is obviously not relevant, so I will not insist on it any further. Namely, I gathered from your questions that you didn't understand what the Cazin Krajina is. It is the north-western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, mostly populated by Muslims, so that you should bear that in mind as we mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was explained it was Bihac. That was of considerable assistance. Yes. Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the north-western part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a pocket there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Kljuic, or, rather, do you know that the intelligence service of the HVO collected data about several thousand Mujahedin with very precise particulars, passport numbers, their countries of origin, and those who acquired citizenship in the BH and that they forwarded them on to the State Department and the CIA? Have you had occasion to see that list?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I didn't know that the intelligence service of Croatia had those records, but it is to be assumed that most of the people came to Bosnia via Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was fear of the Mujahedin not only a real fear but subsequent events made those fears true?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The arrival of the Mujahedins spoiled the multi-ethnic composition of the Bosnian forces, and it did the greatest damage to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement you mentioned in several places that the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a completely independent party which, as a sister, had the HDZ of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: While I was president, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wish to draw your attention to what was said about this by the president of Croatia, Stjepan Mesic, testifying in The Hague in other case. And he says: "Formally I must say for the sake of the truth that the HDZ in Croatia was separate from the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Formally. But in actual fact, all decisions were taken in Zagreb, and I believe that there's no doubt about that. I think there's no point in asking whether the HDZ in Bosnia was an independent party. Formally it was, but in reality, it was not." So is Mesic telling the truth or is what you are saying right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. I must say that I was the first Croat who formulated the interests of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the fall of communism. The gist of my doctrine was a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later on it would become an independent country, and the equality of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which over a period of many years of royalist and communist Yugoslavia, it was not the case. The Croats were not equal, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kljuic. So Mesic is not telling the truth. I see from your statement that you were a great supporter of a united and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you get away with that comment, and it's a pure comment, "Mesic is not telling the truth," that's not what the witness said. He merely gave his own account, and Mr. Mesic no doubt was giving his. Insofar as there is any difference between it, it will be a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine whether there's any significance in it or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to say that what Mr. Milosevic said about Mesic's statement is his view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mine or Mesic's? But I was quoting Mesic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you're now making a general assessment on the basis of a small fragment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not get into this argument. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were a supporter of a sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. You have confirmed that; haven't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what you're claiming. However, during talks among the leaders of the Yugoslav republics regarding the future of the federal state, on behalf of the Bosnian Croats, you asked Tudjman to represent your interests as well. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I have to describe the background. Karadzic officially gave you the right - and there is a written document about that - that you should represent at the federal level the interests of the Bosnian Serbs. Of course, Zagreb demanded the same from me. I didn't provide that in a document, but at meetings at which Bosnian Croats were not represented, this was implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't trust Alija Izetbegovic as the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Regarding the points on which we had agreed prior to those meetings - and that was frequently the case - it was his duty to say that those were the positions upheld by the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, isn't it a little strange, Mr. Kljuic? You fought so much for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina and yet you don't trust the president of the Presidency of that state?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I trusted what had been agreed on, but I wouldn't give anyone a carte blanche to speak in my name and the name of the Bosnian Croats in our absence if we didn't know what the subject of discussion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You've answered that question. Now, tell me, please, since you were speaking about the re-election of Izetbegovic, you say that Karadzic had proposed that since one term had expired for Izetbegovic and that he was a Muslim, that the next in order should be a Croat, and he had proposed you to be elected president of the Presidency. Wasn't it logical for people to rotate every year, that is, that the representatives of all three nations?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was logical, but the constitution allowed for one year plus another year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that Karadzic made this proposal because such a solution suited him as a Croat in that position would not have the support of Zagreb. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He may have not had the support of Zagreb, but he also wouldn't have institutional authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why not if he were to be elected president of the Presidency? Does that mean that this position was reserved for a Muslim representative?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. In a normal situation, had it not been for the war in Croatia and the break-up of Yugoslavia, had it not been for the instrumentalisation of the Yugoslav People's Army, which already then had occupied Bosnia, this rotation could have been done simply, even a year before the constitution allowed Izetbegovic to retain that position. However, with such a backdrop and without having any real impact, I could have been a figurehead in the Presidency for a certain period of time. I could have made press briefings, held press briefings for foreign reporters, but I'm not sure I could have had full support in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does your explanation mean that official Croatia did not want a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina because, as president, would you have had to fight for what you had promised your voters and that is a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Official Croatia changed from time to time the forms of its political activity vis-a-vis Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I, in my communications, always stressed the necessity of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. And even during meetings when opposite views were aired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you believe that the Serbs, since Karadzic on behalf of the Serb side had proposed to you that it was a Croat's turn and that you should be the one as you got more votes than the other two Croats in the Presidency, would then you have remained within a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina? That proposal surely meant that, that this rotation should begin, which would be evidence of the equality of all three peoples.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. Karadzic's intentions were quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but later on it was Karadzic himself who signed, together with representatives of the Croats and Alija Izetbegovic, the Cutileiro plan which spoke of a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Izetbegovic withdrew his signature. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I know about that from the media, because in those days, I was very sick, and during the Lisbon negotiations I was in a Sarajevo hospital in intensive care.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you're aware of the event. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know of the event and the withdrawal of the signature, which was explained by withdrawal of agreement for the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But in the same paragraph, when you talk about your election, you say that you rejected Karadzic's proposal because you knew that the war would come. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, any normal person in those days knew that you and the Yugoslav People's Army would not renounce force, and we were constantly exposed to JNA threats, and under those conditions we were required to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So, Mr. Kljuic, it means you were arming yourselves, the Muslims were arming themselves, and you for a whole five months prior to the outbreak of the war knew that the war would come.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That was quite -- it was quite normal to expect it after everything that had happened in Slovenia, like an operetta. And in Croatia as the greatest tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kljuic. I won't belabour the point any further because it is quite obvious that a process was ongoing conducive to war. But from the basis of the break-up of Yugoslavia. Surely you can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: You must know that on the 19th of December, 1991, both Slovenia and Croatia were outside Yugoslavia, and that vast military troops were present in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and our aim was that we mustn't remain within the Rump Yugoslavia. As for Bosnian policies, it was -- they were the most flexible, and you know that for a time there was an initiative by Gligorov and Izetbegovic for the Yugoslav confederation to be construed in a highly flexible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that very initiative by Izetbegovic and Gligorov was presented at a meeting of six presidents of republics held in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that I, on behalf of Serbia, accepted this construction by Izetbegovic and Gligorov?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the others didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who are those others, then? Izetbegovic and Gligorov are making a proposal. Serbia accepts. I see; Slovenia and Croatia. So Slovenia and Croatia refused such a flexible structure too.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you must know the context. There had already been a lot of destruction in Croatia, the casualties were enormous, and the Croatian people in Croatia, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you're not testifying about Croatia now so let's not waste any more time on that. But is it true that on page 4, paragraph 5 you said that propaganda told the Serbs that they mustn't allow the same to happen to them as had happened during the Second World War? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This need not be attributed just to me. This was a daily -- repeated daily in the papers, on radio and television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Very well. So that's not at issue. Tell me, what happened to the Serbs in the Second World War, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, no, we don't want this. No. Please. Please do not go into it. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kljuic, tell me, since you spoke of the reasons why you clashed with the Serbs, tell me, how did the clash between the Muslims and the Croats break out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think again that we're not concerned with this. Unless there is some particular point concerning yourself that you want to put, Mr. Milosevic, you can, but it doesn't seem to me that it bears any relevance to this particular indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is highly relevant due to the fact that Croatian and Muslim forces were linked by the idea to break up Yugoslavia, and later on they clashed because they couldn't agree in coordinating their mutual interests.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not the competent person to answer this question because I already -- I was no longer a leader of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that the JNA was the only recognised armed force in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout 1991, which means it was at home in 1991.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, while it behaved in conformity with the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, did official units of the Croatian army, were they involved in the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not just in 1992 but in 1993, 1994, et cetera? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't have information about that, but it is highly probable that they were present, that is, units were present. But I have to tell you that they were always composed of Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the Croats from other parts of the area were not too willing to wage war for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Kljuic, I have here a letter, since I'm asking you about it, a letter which Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, signed and addressed to Klaus Kinkel and Peter Kooijmans. "Gentlemen," et cetera. And then in the third paragraph it says, in the second: "The term a Muslim offensive is inappropriate because though in the army of BH Muslims are dominant, it is not a Muslim army, nor, therefore, is it a Muslim offensive. Then the term Croatian towns is inappropriate because these are towns with mixed populations with a minimum majority of Croats. Those towns are in central Bosnia and have now been ethnically cleansed of Muslims." And then in the fourth paragraph, it says: "Croatia already has six brigades engaged in Bosnia and Herzegovina through special purpose units, tanks, helicopters, artillery, and officers of the Croatian army have been appointed to command positions in the HVO. For example, Ante Roso has been appointed main commander of the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he complains of this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the date -- what was the date of the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, now that's something that I wanted to ask you most particularly, Mr. May, because without a doubt this is an original letter. I recognise the signature of Alija Izetbegovic. I was provided it by Mr. Nice's side, and the number is 01826430, but quite obviously it has been copied in such a way that the date does not exist, and disclosed to me by the opposite side. So please would you have this exhibited with respect to the things it says and in order to ascertain and establish why the opposite side is redacting documents in such a way as the date is obliterated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all -- we'll deal with it in this way: First of all, Mr. Kljuic, do you know anything about the matter that the accused has been reading out? It's an undated letter, apparently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only assume that the letter was dated -- dates to 1993 when I held no political position. But the relationships between the Croats and the Muslims - today the Bosniaks - must be viewed within the context of numerous secret meetings and decisions that they had between themselves, between the president of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, and the presiding person of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.
