Only when you have an insight into their documents -- or if I had an insight into those documents would I be able to assess the global situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider this document at the end of the evidence. We will not take up time with it now, decide whether we should exhibit it or not. And we'll hear from the Prosecution about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we see it so we can see if we can dig it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Pass it to the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, tell me now, please, Mr. Kljuic - and this was during your time, 1992 - who first shelled Serb villages in Bosanska Posavina and from which vantage point? Was it the Croatian army across the River Sava?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you know nothing about that act of aggression across the Sava River or from across the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: All I know is that in 1991, from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina - and we had no control over it - there was shooting onto the Republic of Croatia from BH territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is what I read out correct, what Izetbegovic says in his letter, that individual towns in Central Bosnia had been ethnically cleansed by the army of Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't know about it in that form but that there was ethnic cleansing on the Croatian side, that cannot be denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Is it true and correct that it was precisely these Mujahedin, the ones that I mentioned but as you say you don't know about them, that the army, the Muslim army, ethnically cleansed Central Bosnia of its Croatian citizens?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It is true that the Mujahedin were used only against the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, please, do you know, for example, about or know of -- actually, take a look at these two documents, please. Sarajevo the 29th of May, 1992 is the date, and these documents speak about the specifications or the requirements for Bosnia-Herzegovina prepared by Azim Karamehmedovic and approved by President Alija Izetbegovic, and the signature is -- with his signature. And then it testifies to 2 million bullets, rifles, et cetera, et cetera, the specifications and positions are listed. And that is May 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Are these then -- just give us your opinion: Are these authentic documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- that via Slovenia they are asking for the following?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Izetbegovic is in fact requesting equipment from Slovenia. And it's the letter which refers to Jansa [phoen].

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This is not unnatural in anyway. You don't suppose, I assume, that we waited, stood around waiting to be killed by the JNA without looking for a way out in the form of procuring weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish and don't interrupt him. You're putting these serious matters to him. He should have a chance to deal with them. Yes. Go on. Go on, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally, had I had the chance of asking the devil for weapons, I would have asked him to give me them to defend myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So when it comes to a question of Croats and Muslims, then your defence is -- well, during the war between the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was defending themselves from whom, from the Serbs, or were you defending yourselves from the Muslims, you Croats, I mean?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me about something that was the most difficult times for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that war between the Croats and the Muslims, and that was mostly made use of, benefited your ideas. And on the 18th of March, 1994, I was -- I saw the truce being signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your answer is quite different. It's not what I asked you. So as a member of the Presidency, you knew about this procurement, did you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know about it because it wasn't decided at the level of the Presidency. And above all, because Alija Izetbegovic went against the constitution, the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, violated it. And in practical terms, he disposed of the money and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kljuic. Is it true that you, for your part, you personally, and although you mention somebody here as being an HDZ extremist, you appointed Mate Boban for Herzegovina and Iko Stanic for Posavina, when it came to this organisation and all the rest of it, everything that was to follow?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. I was the political leader of the HDZ party, and I didn't deal with these practical matters. Now, as we had two set regions with a concentrated Croatian population, that it was quite normal that Iko Stanic should see to those operational matters in Posavina and Mate Boban should do the same in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean without a doubt that as this took place when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been established, that throughout that time during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there we saw the existence of two armies, actually, within that Bosnia and Herzegovina? We had the Croatian side and the Muslim side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were armed forces of -- what did exist was the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the official title for all the formations that stood up to the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And the HVO. Was the HVO within the frameworks of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It was within the armed forces, which meant all units of Bosnia-Herzegovina defending the country. The HVO, HOS, and the Territorial Defence who grew to become the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the HVO had the clash and conflict and when it defended Croatian settlements from a Muslim attack, it was also within the composition of the BH army then too.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, in formal terms, yes, but a conflict broke out. There was a clash.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was a clash within one army, according to what you're saying, a clash within a single army?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way, but from time to time they had quite different relationships. For example, in 1995, they would act together again, pool their efforts again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this came under outside pressure, under the effects of outside pressure.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I wasn't in Geneva, London or Dayton. You didn't see me there because I was a Bosnian Herzegovinian integralist and I was opposed to many people and thus eliminated from the negotiating teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this now, please: Did you, as a leader of the Bosnian Croats, did you do anything to prevent the conflict from breaking out at all or is it quite clear that the conflict came into being because of pressure exerted by Islamic fundamentalism and the large great crimes committed against the Croats at that period?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The conflict was quite -- there was no understanding for the conflict, and although I did not have a single official post to play, I did what I could in a Sarajevo under siege. I did what I could to lessen the tensions. Unfortunately, I was not successful in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you claim that from positions of president of the HDZ you were replaced because of the lack of extremism in your positions when it came to the fate of the Croatian people in the BH.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here a statement by you given -- actually, it's a newspaper statement, one to the press. It is 01819856 is the ERN number, and it is your interview, in fact. And you say: "Izetbegovic did not inform me that the SDA in July 1991 had set up a council for the defence. Muslim nationalists still claim today that I advocated a division of Bosnia." And then you say: "I had to recognise Herceg-Bosna for its advocates to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is that right, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to explain that, what I mean -- meant by that statement. The statement is a concise one but with enormous consequences. Yes, it is true that Izetbegovic did not inform me that he had set up some kind of a military council. A part from the extremist Muslim political leaders kept accusing me of dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas on the 18th of November, 1991, without my approval and permission and without my presence, in fact, Herceg-Bosna was established as a counterbalance to the already-formed Serb autonomous Krajinas at the time. Quite simply, the Croats, especially in Herzegovina where they were the strongest, wanted to have what the Serbs had, and so they found the same formula for doing that. However, we represented that organisation as being one without any military characteristics, as an association catering to the life of the population in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm talking about the secret Muslim organisation, because from the transcript of the testimony here, it says -- we can see that the lawyer -- I don't know the man but I can see from the report with respect to your testimony -- that lawyer Naumovski went back to the arming of Bosnia-Herzegovina and asked Kljuic whether he knew that the Muslims, on the 10th of June 1991, established a Muslim defence council. And Kljuic's answer was that he did not know about its establishment, and the lawyer put forward a document of the SDA party which confirmed his words, and this document was signed by Hasan Cengic. The council noted that this was the first secret military organisation on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that right, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: May I explain what this was all about? I was interrupted on how I recognised Herceg-Bosna in order for them to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina. As this organisation, this association at the time did not have any secessionist character with respect to the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I as the president and behind whose back all this was done, said the following: "If you are creating that within Bosnia-Herzegovina, then I can approve your organisation," and I was being told that everything was being done within Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as the documents that Mr. Milosevic is mentioning, I really didn't know about that organisation, no, and I don't think that that's a crime on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Of course it's not a sin or crime on your part for not having known that, Mr. Kljuic. I'm trying to establish the facts and not to accuse you of anything, accuse you for not knowing things. Now, judging from the documents I've been disclosed here, this is a portion of some stenographic notes from a Presidency meeting of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says Stjepan Kljuic, and the number, Mr. May, is 018243838. Paragraph 2. The opposite side just provides us with some excerpts, but quite evidently, this has been extracted from the original stenographic notes. It says Stjepan Kljuic, in paragraph 2, where he says: "Doko told me --" and Doko is the Defence Minister, right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he's the man who was in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say: "Doko told me about his conversation with Arkan. He does not recognise either Milosevic or Karadzic, but in this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say the western part where Tomislavgrad, Kupres and all the other places, I think these people are still subordinated to the party leaders." And then you go on to say: "Whether we wish to acknowledge this or not, we must talk to Arkan because he holds the power in his hands." So therefore, quite clearly you were informed that Serbia had nothing at all to do with what was going on over there.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I would accept that if you were to convince me that Arkan was not acting under your command or the command of some military formation or other in the then-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you yourself have just said it. And then on that same -- in those same stenographic notes, Plavsic makes a comment and asks who is commanding the TO. Izetbegovic says Vukosavljevic is the commander of the TO. And then Ejub Ganic takes the floor, and there's some sort of map where the weapons were provided and Vucurevic has everything in Krajina. The Muslims feel that the Serbs have used up their quota whereas the others have not. And Nikola's idea is a good one, to take it back. Nikola Koljevic, they mean. Nikola Koljevic at that meeting is proposing that the weapons be withdrawn from all three sides, all three parties. If some quota had been provided them from the Territorial Defence stockpiles.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: You must know that Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina was engulfed by great misfortune, the fact that their communists had agreed to having the weapons belonging to the Territorial Defence handed over to the JNA. And, Your Honours, you will see within the concepts of Yugoslavia's security that there existed official Yugoslav troops, Yugoslav JNA troops on the one hand and the weapons which the citizens had procured and purchased for themselves to use it when the time came, first and foremost should there be an aggression against Yugoslavia. However, apart from a decision on the reorganisation of the army when Sarajevo was no longer an army region, the greatest handicap was that vast quantities of weapons of the Territorial Defence were ceded to the Yugoslav People's Army. As tensions heightened and as incidents multiplied, the army took advantage of the situation to selectively distribute mostly to the Serbs part of the Territorial Defence, allegedly to return it to them. Of course, they didn't do the same to -- with respect to the Croats and the Muslims and this further endangered peace in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kljuic. Since you say that these volunteers from Serbia were under somebody's supervision, although you yourself say what Doko told you, I have here in a binder disclosed to me, but unfortunately there's no number here though I received it from the side opposite. It is the Presidency of the HDZ for the republic Crisis Staff, the 8th of October, 1991. And among other things, in the Conclusions, point 10, it says in municipalities with volunteers lists of volunteers must be made and provided to the Republican Crisis Staff to be sent to crisis areas. So you're organising the dispatch of volunteered to Croatia, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. This wasn't a matter of policy. Volunteers from Bosnia-Herzegovina went to Croatia in very large numbers. There was no need to mobilise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, question -- doesn't that also apply to Serbia, that it wasn't a matter of policy, but that volunteers were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have here, Mr. May, I didn't notice 005700593, and this is on the next page of that same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you a few more things, Mr. Kljuic. There really is no marking here. It talks about command responsibility. It's an article in these binders, I'm sure you will remember. "The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Durakovic, Mirko Mijatovic [phoen], Ivo Komsic, and Stjepan Kljuic signed an announcement warning of the instrumentalisation of religion for political purposes and the Islamisation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Did you sign this announcement, together with the other members of the Presidency protesting against the Islamisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then there's no need to dwell on that any further. Let me just ask you also, Mr. Kljuic, what do you know about camps in Bosnia and Herzegovina? That is in the territory under Muslim control and for a time also under your and Muslim combined control?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: As far as camps are concerned, I can only talk about Sarajevo. There were cases of forcible mobilisation of people to perform physical work, manual work, and there were also certain groups that would occasionally unlawfully arrest certain citizens. Such a practice was continued in particular during 1993. And one of my pre-conditions for rejoining the Presidency in October 1993 was that all those armed groups who were not acting as part of a system of the army be arrested, or which --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Kljuic. I'm asking you about something else. I have here stenographic notes of a meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina that you attended. I didn't get it from the side opposite so I will give it to you to identify. Your presence is visible. There's nothing that you say that I wish to challenge, but your presence Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is evident. These are transcripts from a meeting of the Presidency held on the 26th of April, 1994, when there is a reference to the detention of people. And because my time is short, I will give you the entire stenographic notes to be read and admitted into evidence, because you were present at that meeting. Alija Izetbegovic, the president, says, "I am not sure that it is their fault." He's talking about people who had been unlawfully arrested. Pazaric, Konjic, Tarcin, Hrasnica. All these things were mentioned at a meeting of the Presidency, and these were all camps held by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And he says, "I'm not sure that they're guilty in the legal sense of the word. Those in Tarcin, they were kept there as a countermeasure to those in Hadzici." And in Hadzici there was a Serb-held prison, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that this is actually a concentration camp or a collection camp. So they're in a different form. They're not guilty in the legal sense. It's a measure. It's a measure for a measure, as they say. Measure for measure. You have no way of liberating those people. So is it clear from this that at a meeting of the Presidency this was discussed, which means that they were aware of it. There's mention made of some people being held up to two years without having been put on trial at all. The president says Hrasnica, Konjic, Tarcin, and others are mentioned, and if we release those men, they will not release those others from Kule. Actually, those people are outside the law, et cetera. And then he says this is virtually a concentration came, whereas in fact it's a collection centre. So do you know what was discussed, though it wasn't the most important issue? The first agenda item was the appointment of ambassadors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us now stop for a moment. Let the witness see the copy of the notes at least to identify them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are tape recordings, transcripts of tape recordings. I would just keep the last portion from these stenographic notes and then I'll hand the rest over to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour, I wish to finish what I was saying before I was interrupted. My return to the Presidency was conditioned by me by the elimination of irregular troops which engaged in arrests of people, of citizens. I have to tell you that this was done at the time. This was the first time in these parts for the legal authorities to react to groups which acted contrary to the law. Even today, I do not believe that the scope of these measures was appropriate, but what was done in Sarajevo at the time restored faith in the security and safety of citizens. As regards the stenographic notes offered by Mr. Milosevic, the date is April 1994 when it was already becoming clear to me in particular, because this was a period several months into my renewed membership in the Presidency, when we were receiving information from various sides that there were camps or prisons, which is quite irrelevant and unimportant how you call those facilities, but facilities in which Serbs were held, and not just captured soldiers, Serb citizens. So there's no doubt that I and most of the members of the Presidency were against this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I suspect the purpose is to get the notes in front of us, but thank you for making plain your position. Now, Mr. Milosevic, have you got anything else you want to ask the witness? You've had rather longer than the time that we allotted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your generosity, Mr. May, but I really do have more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, do you remember that at that same meeting - and this is the final part of the stenographic notes that I wish to tender - mention was made of Sefer Halilovic and his rank. He was first at the head of the army, then he was released because of some conflict with Izetbegovic, then there was some discussion as to a high rank that he should be awarded. Do you remember that was also discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There was a problem as to how to maintain the dignity of that particular individual who had virtually been replaced from a position of leadership. But that wasn't a general issue. It was a question of the relationship between Halilovic and Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would just read a small quotation from Izetbegovic for you to confirm the content, as he also spoke about, as he puts it, arguments in favour and against the appointment. He says: "However, because of that first period of time when he did quite a lot for the army, and particularly before the war in organising the army, I at least know him at least six months prior to the war, at least from October prior to the war as one of the leading people who then organised the resistance in 1991." This is something that I could confirm. There are some printing errors, of course, in the grammar, but it's clear. He worked in the army up until May 1993, et cetera, et cetera. So Izetbegovic himself is confirming that six months prior to the outbreak of the war, the army was organised, and he attributes great merit for this to Sefer Halilovic as an argument in favour of him having to be given an appropriate status or treatment, et cetera. So my question -- the point of my question is: Is this without doubt -- does this show without doubt that six months prior to the outbreak of the war the Muslim army in Bosnia-Herzegovina was organised?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Believe me, Izetbegovic was bragging. There was no army. If only there had been, then Sarajevo would have been defended better, there would have been less casualties. You know what people are like. When it was said that military years of service would be recognised, there were people who applied claiming that they had fought from I don't know when. But this was not relevant when talking about the overall strength of our military forces as compared to the JNA in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think this must be your last question because we have to be out of here before 2.00. So you could certainly ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about a letter which Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic, as members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, addressed to the Federal Secretary for National Defence and in which they voice their position regarding the need to preserve Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I was not given that letter, and I can't quote from it any other parts except those quoted by Mr. Nice when he was examining you. Are you familiar with that letter?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. That letter was published in the newspapers. Simply in a sense they were bringing pressure to bear on General Kadijevic for the army to act with more resoluteness because it is supported by all Yugoslav-minded people, which was not the truth, because at least with regard to the three western republics, there weren't many Yugoslav-minded citizens except most of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which considered the Yugoslav army to be their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that Yugoslav oriented citizens did not support the JNA?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that they did but they were fewer and fewer in number. You must know when this was happening. This was at the time when it became clear to everyone that Yugoslavia, in the way that you were leading it, could not be preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After this letter that you say was written in September, which is probably true though I don't have it, said that on the 24th of December, 1991, you went to a meeting or, rather, they came to a meeting with you in Sarajevo - that is the military leadership, the army leadership - and they discussed some common problems with the top leaders of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were two questions addressed: First what Yugoslavia would look like because Slovenia and Croatia had still not seceded. This happened on the 15th of January, 1992. Secondly, there was a debate as to how Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state would relate to the army belonging to it, because you must know that as a state we wanted to accept all the units which, according to establishment, belonged to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were just against detachments of the army coming from other parts of Yugoslavia but those that were stationed in Bosnia-Herzegovina during normal deployment of the army, we accepted them as our army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Kljuic, you're saying three western republics. Somewhere in the statement you will remember - I can't waste time to find the exact spot - you said that those three western republics took positions that they felt that they were damaged economically in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you claim that of Bosnia-Herzegovina when it is well known that Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a republic as a whole, was treated as an underdeveloped region and received the lion's share of the federal fund for aid to the underdeveloped regions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Half of it was used to finance it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the last question and last answer. Yes, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to explain, Your Honours, that this was in the context of a socialist planned economy. Bosnia and Herzegovina had the largest military purpose industry, wartime industry, which it did not export itself, but it exported those products through the Defence Ministry of Yugoslavia, the SSNO. We manufactured tanks for a small sum of money and they sold them for a much bigger sum to the non-aligned countries. We had energy resources and timber, and those prices were reduced because of internal relationships within Yugoslavia. To all intents and purposes, Bosnia and Herzegovina already then could have lived independently, but conscious of the fact that the prices of Bosnian products were intentionally depressed, such as timber, coal, energy, and military products, the Yugoslav federation, through the fund for underdeveloped republics and provinces compensated Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you say that those prices were down because of any Serbian policy when half of the electric energy in Yugoslavia was manufactured in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I didn't say because of Serbian policy. It was the Yugoslav state policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I think we'll have to call that a day and we'll consider the position. Mr. Nice, the witness can't come back tomorrow, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me just find out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shan't be here tomorrow, that's not critical, not necessarily, but the witness, I know, wishes to get back tomorrow and is expecting to go back tomorrow, he has duties to perform. There is a sort of fundamental problem as well about the time that witnesses take. Now, I know that this is a sensitive issue for the Trial Chamber, but as you will appreciate, we are now -- we're having to axe basically by half our witness list in order to finish in time. We're making selections. Now, this witness has already -- and I took this witness very shortly. In the event, I produced very few exhibits, and I took him for a limited number of purposes. His cross-examination, I think, is now almost getting on for twice as much as the examination-in-chief, and can I just explain the problem that we're having --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm not sure this is the right moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have no doubt there is a problem. Let us just deal with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm afraid we can't permit, for reasons of time, any examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Not even two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is something very important. I need two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sure it is. But we don't have the time. We have other matters we have to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's just one question I want to ask him about one particular meeting, whether he knows or not about it. One question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There are some documents --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just give these documents in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There are documents which need to be put in, and we will deal with that. I think you have three documents. Let the registrar tell us what she has. There's the undated document at the beginning. Mr. Nice, you saw that undated document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It went back. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was something disclosed by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Something disclosed and I think we have yet to track it down with the number on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 164 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the other documents were -- the other documents were, and of course they're in B/C/S so I can't now identify them. There was the letter from Alija Izetbegovic. Yes, I do remember that. There was -- or referring to Alija Izetbegovic. Mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Defence Exhibit 165 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And finally, there were the stenographic notes which can be exhibited. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I should identify the tabs that were exhibited in the Prosecution's bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the final Defence number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 165, Your Honour -- Defence Exhibit 166, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Nice, if you would do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask that you allow, although I didn't formally produce it, the summary background, the history of the witness, that's number 1, for the ones that have been produced, the number 2, tab 2, 8, 15, 18, and 20; so I'd ask that number 1 be added to those. The map. No. Quite right. There is no 20, the map had its own separate number. I should have known that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the only ones to be produced are 1, 2, 8, 15, 18. The map's already been produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would just like to attach the rest of these stenographic notes as Mr. Kljuic confirmed that they too became clear that -- that it became clear to them too that Serbian civilians were being held in camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that. And tomorrow morning, we will begin with the 92 bis statements, the motion for application to let them in, and we'll then continue with the evidence. And in due course, you can address us on the question of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One sentence, and it will make sense immediately and it's this: The sort of problems with quantities of cross-examination for witnesses like this are inevitably inclining us in our selection against more interesting witnesses, and that's the problem we face. And it's very difficult because we regularly, on a daily basis almost, are trying to hack away at the list, and both predictability and time taken -- predictability of time to be taken and problems with this type of witness are causing us great difficulties. I just thought I'd mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kljuic, I'm sorry you've been kept waiting during that debate, but the fact is your evidence is now concluded. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you are free to go. And we're going to adjourn too. We'll return the big binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of July, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
